articles.title: DOJ to form panel to vet Truth Commission findings on drug war killings
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) will form a fact-finding panel to review the Truth Commission's report on drug war killings under the Duterte administration, following the presentation of the…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 4:24pm

The Department of Justice (DOJ) will form a fact-finding panel to review the Truth Commission's report on drug war killings under the Duterte administration, following the presentation of the commission's preliminary findings.

Speaking at the Truth Commission's national conference on Monday, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said the DOJ would need to thoroughly examine the evidence gathered by the commission to ensure that any charges eventually filed in court would be strong enough to withstand legal scrutiny.

"Yes, definitely we will have a panel to review everything because we will check on the verifiable facts. What are the pieces of evidence? Are they purely testimonial? Are they purely physical evidence?” Vida said.
“The whole gamut, the whole spectrum, right? Because we don't want to file weak cases if ever they will be filed,” he added.
During the conference, former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge and current Truth Commission chairperson Raul Pangalangan presented the group's initial findings.

While emphasizing that the report was still preliminary, the commission said the evidence gathered was already sufficient to conclude that the drug war killings under former President Rodrigo Duterte were “state-organized.”
It also said the government's “official account cannot be accepted at face value” and that, in cases brought forward by victims' families, “no one has been held to account.”
The Truth Commission also presented the following key findings:

items: 8,320 documented killings, a figure expected to increase
Victims were overwhelmingly men of working and parenting age
Killings were concentrated in urban communities
Operations began almost everywhere at once and followed the police
Many killings bore the marks of execution
The official “manlaban” account did not hold up
Official records were incomplete and at times unreliable
Families had effectively carried out the State's investigative work
The drug war did not end in 2022
The commission proposed 27 reforms, five of which it said could not wait

blocks.text: Challenges in case build-up
The DOJ acknowledged that building cases from the available evidence would be challenging, particularly in establishing the credibility and admissibility of accounts provided by victims' families.
“Yes, very challenging, kasi yung sinabi nila kanina eh di ba kapag victim, totoo naman to eh, ‘Sabi kasi nung ano nakaluhod na yung anak ko nung binaril.’ Sabi nga nila. Di ba hearsay?” Vida said.
(Yes, very challenging, because, as mentioned earlier, a family member might say, ‘Someone told me my child was already kneeling when he was shot.’ Isn't that hearsay?)
"Who was actually there when it happened? These are the challenges in conducting the investigation and building up a case," he added.
Duterte is currently detained at the ICC detention facility in The Hague, with his trial proper for crimes against humanity scheduled to begin on November 30.
Vida said he was not in favor of holding local proceedings simultaneously with the ICC trial, stressing that the DOJ must first determine the appropriate legal strategy.

“I don't like simultaneous proceedings. That's different, right? Because you're running into the possibility of a conflict. It could be complementary, or it could involve sequencing. It depends on the proper and appropriate legal strategy,” he said.
The Justice secretary said the department remained committed to fulfilling its mandate “for the people and by the people.”— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Constitutional law expert brands defence bill allowing secret security rules ‘lazy and irresponsible’
articles.summary:
Anne Twomey says lack of proper debate around bill is ‘flabbergasting’ amid concerns over extension of ministerial powers

Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one…

blocks.text: Labor’s new defence bill is “lazy and irresponsible” lawmaking, one of Australia’s leading constitutional scholars has warned, claiming provisions for the government to secretly class any facility as a special security zone could raise serious legal issues.

Prime minister Anthony Albanese claimed on Monday that critics of the ‘accelerating capability and protecting bases’ bill were “jump[ing] at shadows”, accusing them of “absurd” claims. But parliamentary crossbenchers opposed to the bill, which was rushed through parliament with little public scrutiny, were joined on Monday by Prof Anne Twomey, who expressed alarm about what she called an increasing trend of ministers exercising discretionary powers without parliamentary oversight.

“Yes it’s important we have defence legislation that’s flexible to deal with uncertain times, but let’s remember we’re trying to defend our democratic system of government, and we don’t want to throw it out at the same time,” Twomey told Guardian Australia.

In a video on her Youtube channel, Twomey – professor emerita at the University of Sydney – claimed it was “flabbergasting that it was not the subject of proper debate or scrutiny before this law was enacted”.
“This notion of permitting secret alterations to commonwealth, state and territory laws is a really serious development.”

The wide-ranging bill criminalises entering or photographing a defence security zone or a person or thing within, entering or leaving it, with a maximum penalty of up to seven years’ jail time, a $152,880 fine, or both. Security zones can include regular defence bases but can also extend to emergency, temporary or mobile sites as decided by a minister, with wide-ranging powers to “effectively do anything”.

The minister can make a “capability declaration”, which allows for certain activity to be carried out “without contravening certain other laws, or changes the way that other laws apply” – including state and territory laws. Such a declaration can also be held back from being declared as a legislative instrument.

After passing the Senate last week, the final bill passed the lower house on Monday evening. Labor and the Coalition supported the bill, with only a handful of crossbenchers – including Kate Chaney, Monique Ryan and Andrew Wilkie – resisting.

The Greens, David Pocock, Digital Rights Watch and other civil society groups also strongly opposed the bill. But Albanese, in his first public comments on the legislation, said “people shouldn’t jump at shadows”, claiming the powers were necessary and “just practical”.
“It will be accountable obviously for things that are designated, but we live in unsafe times,” he said on Monday.

“I find it remarkable in 2026, there’s a question over whether we need to designate areas as being protected. And we live in times where we know there are more conflicts in the world today than at any time since World War II.”
Greens leader David Shoebridge called the changes “extreme wartime powers”, and “an assault on civil liberties”, claiming people may be charged for breaking laws they weren’t even aware of.
Pocock said Albanese’s response was “disingenuous”.

“We need to protect sensitive defence facilities from threats posed by drones and other technologies. But that doesn’t mean handing the defence minister extraordinary powers without proper safeguards,” he told Guardian Australia.
“At a bare minimum, far stronger safeguards are needed around the use of ministerial powers, the need to protect civil liberties and greater transparency.”

Twomey, in her video, branded the legislation “quite disturbing”, noting declarations could be made secretly – which she said raised “serious rule of law issues” – and called out what she said was a concerning movement of giving ministers more discretionary power.

“Instead of working out what laws need to change to accommodate defence needs and then balancing them against the needs and rights of the community, the parliament has effectively just given up and instead given the power to the minister or indeed senior public servants or defence officers to make decisions that exclude the application of existing laws to defence activities.
“This is a lazy and irresponsible abandonment by parliament of both its scrutiny and its lawmaking roles, raising the risk that these powers will be misused in the future.”

articles.summary: Alice Huang was in touch with an officer from China's Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, a New York Times report says

blocks.text: ALICE HUANG. A screengrab from CTI video footage obtained November 9, 2026 shows a woman identified by Reuters as Alice Huang after comparison with a photograph obtained separately, attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (in black) at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan May 22, 2025.
CTI via REUTERS TV
Alice Huang was in touch with an officer from China's Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, a New York Times report says

items: Alice Huang, linked to Nvidia's scandal, maintained contact with a Chinese spy agency official for over a year during her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang, according to a New York Times report.
US authorities are investigating Megaspeed International, a company previously led by Alice Huang, for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China, while doubts remain about her being a spy.
The scandal has raised questions about US export controls on China, with bipartisan lawmakers suggesting the previous administration may have been too lenient.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – Alice Huang, the Chinese woman at the heart of Nvidia’s recent scandal, kept in contact with an official from China’s top spy agency for more than a year during her affair with former CEO Jensen Huang, the New York Times reported on Sunday, November 22.

Alice Huang was in touch with an officer from China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the report said, citing people with knowledge of intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

A spokesperson for Jensen Huang declined to comment. Spokespeople for Nvidia and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters has not been able to reach Alice Huang for comment.
Alice Huang previously led Singapore-based Megaspeed International, an important Nvidia customer that once accounted for billions in Nvidia chip sales.
US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over concerns it smuggled Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China.
Sunday’s report comes as US officials have cast doubt on initial suggestions that Alice Huang was a spy, as the newspaper reported last month.
That October 29 article touched off a scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s resignation two weeks later and a steep drop in Nvidia’s stock price.
Trump administration officials have repeatedly said they have not concluded that Alice Huang spied for China.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said this month the Justice Department had not yet reached a conclusion on whether she was a Chinese spy.
US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton repeated that on Sunday.

“Attorney General Blanche has been very clear that this is a matter under investigation, both Ms Huang and her company, for various matters,” Clayton told CNN’s “State of the Union” program. “And I’m going to let that investigation play out.”

The scandal has also prompted a deeper look at Washington’s approach to export controls on China, with lawmakers from both parties questioning whether the Trump administration has been too lax on enforcement and regulation of the prized semiconductors.
The affair between the two itself is of less interest, Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, told NBC’s “Meet the Press.”
“I hope he had a good time,” Kennedy said on Sunday. “It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: PNP on alert ahead of VP Sara impeachment verdict, says DILG chief
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police was instructed to prepare for the worst-case scenario ahead of the eventual impeachment verdict on Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 3:31pm

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla and Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. holds a press conference at the PNP headquarters in Camp Crame, Quezon City on May 10, 2026.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police was instructed to prepare for the worst-case scenario ahead of the eventual impeachment verdict on Vice President Sara Duterte.

In an ambush interview with reporters on Monday, November 23, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said he had told the police to brace for the outcome, as the verdict could stir intense emotions among both Duterte's supporters and critics.
“Dapat ikalma nila (PNP) 'yung mga tao kasi in political trials like that, emotions get very high on both sides so dapat gawin ng pulis gigitna para hindi magkagulo,” Remulla added.
(They need to calm people down because in political trials like that, emotions run very high on both sides, so the police must stand in the middle to prevent chaos).
"We always expect the worst. Wala naman expect na best dito sa PNP eh. We always anticipate, we always prepare,” he added.
(There is no expecting the best here in the PNP. We always anticipate, we always prepare.)

While Remulla said the PNP is preparing for every eventuality, he expressed confidence that the public would ultimately respect the Senate impeachment court's decision, noting that many Filipinos have likely already formed their own conclusions throughout the proceedings

“Alam na nila kung ano ang totoo at hindi. I think sa sarili nilang puso at sa isip humusga na sila so tingin ko handa na rin naman lahat tanggapin kung ano ang magiging hatol ng ating Senado,” Remulla said.
(In their own hearts and minds, they have already judged, so I think everyone is ready to accept whatever the verdict of our Senate will be.)

The Senate impeachment court, which is set to resume hearings on December 1, is currently hearing Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which tackles the vice president's alleged ill-gotten wealth and irregularities in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.

articles.title: Clubs and families revolt as Football Queensland charges $5 a head to watch children play
articles.summary:
Gate fee comes on top of annual cost of between $300 and $700 per family

  • Get our breaking news email,

blocks.text: Football clubs representing hundreds of thousands of players are preparing to break away from Football Queensland this week, saying the state governing body charges unreasonably high fees and is unaccountable.
Some parents and siblings are charged a $5 gate fee to watch children’s matches in parts of regional Queensland.

The gate fee comes on top of an annual cost of between $300 and $700 per family, depending on player age, club and other factors, and a range of other fees, fines and charges. Many football club members say they see little in return for the thousands they pay in fees.
Jessy Mulla is president of Leichhardt Football Club Cairns Incorporated, which was recently disaffiliated from the statewide body.

Football Queensland, which manages the club, introduced a gate fee in 2024 in order to pay for improvements to the ground, Endeavour Park, in Manunda, such as cleaning toilets, employing a full-time gardener, and “increased shade structures and grandstands”, at a quoted price of $20,000 each.
With a few hundred people attending most weekends, the amount raised through gate fees must be substantial, Mulla said.
But there had been “very, very” little improvement to the ground since, Mulla said.
“That’s why everyone asks where’s the money being spent? Where’s the money that gets raised? Where is it going?”
Under Football Queensland’s policy, registered coaches and team managers, referees, volunteers and children under 15 enter free. Pensioners get a discount, paying $4.

The sport’s governing body in the state is a member of the national football body, Football Australia. It provides a range of services for typically volunteer-run clubs, including managing competitions, governance, and developing player professional pathways, as well as managing some facilities.
Clubs have to pay an annual fee to affiliate with the central body, which they pass on to players.

A spokesperson for Football Queensland said the body was “continuing to progress the delivery and investment of long-term infrastructure projects and facility enhancements” in line with its regional facility master plan.

The spokesperson said three levels of government had invested $7.9m into regional Football Queensland facilities since 2023. The central body had also contributed $4.9m in operational costs and capital investment in regional Queensland during the same period, they said.
“A $5 gate fee (or $80 season pass) is consistent with other sporting codes and contributes to FQ’s master plan delivery, helping to offset grounds maintenance and operational expenses,” they said.

It recently created controversy by proposing to charge a $35 per player fee for summer competitions organised by the clubs themselves, and proposing other fee increases, which have since been dropped.
A rebel faction of football clubs is preparing to break away from Football Queensland this week, complaining of a lack of input and transparency of the central body.
Bardon Latrobe football club president, Gerard Doyle, said more than 100 clubs – a majority – had joined a movement pushing for reform.
after newsletter promotion
Doyle estimated that the breakaway clubs represented more than 100,000 football players.
The group is now negotiating with the central body via a law firm. Others were on the fence, he said.
According to its bylaws, Football Queensland’s governing committee must hold elections for new board members this month.
But the board has yet to call elections.
Doyle said that it was now impossible for the board to meet its bylaws, given the need for a one-week period for people to nominate.
Meanwhile, clubs have been given until Wednesday, 25 November, to re-affiliate with the central authority, after an extension to the sign-up period.
Clubs have two options, he said.
“Number one is Football Australia comes in today or tomorrow, two days, and says we will facilitate open and free elections,” he said.
If that doesn’t happen, the clubs will refuse to affiliate and pay their fees and instead create their own rival central body, he said.
“I sound like I’m in a dictatorship in an African nation here, fighting for basic rights.
“To me, it just feels, I’m going to say un-Australian … it’s undemocratic.”

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Marcoleta plunder case has not been dismissed
articles.summary: In a November 23 ruling, the Sandiganbayan denied Marcoleta’s bail petition, with the court finding strong evidence of guilt against him — the threshold of evidence required for bail petitions

blocks.text: Claim: The plunder case against Senator Rodante Marcoleta has been dismissed.

Why we fact-checked this: A reel posted on November 18 by the Facebook page Norbel Vidal shows Marcoleta standing at a lectern, with the text, “Demurrer to Evidence — tapos na ang kaso. Dismissed agad!”
(Demurrer to Evidence — the case is over. Dismissed immediately!)
Additional text overlaid on the reel hints at Marcoleta’s supposed return to office now that the case against him has been junked.

Several social media users welcomed the alleged development in the senator’s case, with some expressing their support for Marcoleta. As of writing, the post has garnered over 148,000 views, 4,200 reactions, 210 comments, and 369 shares.
The facts: There is no court ruling, official statement, or credible report showing that Marcoleta’s case has been dismissed.

The reel was referring to a legal move by Marcoleta and his three co-accused — former lawmaker Michael Defensor and businessmen Aristotle Viray and Joseph Espiritu — who are seeking the dismissal of the P75-million plunder case against them.
On November 11, Sandiganbayan 3rd Division Clerk of Court Dennis Pulma confirmed that Marcoleta and his co-accused had filed motions for leave to file a demurrer to evidence.
A demurrer to evidence asks a court to dismiss a case on the ground that the prosecution’s evidence is insufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
The misleading reel, however, frames Marcoleta’s legal move as though the court had already ruled to dismiss the plunder case.

Contrary to the claim, the senator’s case remains active. On November 23, the anti-graft court’s 3rd Division denied Marcoleta’s petition for bail, ruling that the evidence of guilt against him is strong — the threshold of evidence required for bail petitions.
This ruling, however, is not a guilty verdict against Marcoleta and his co-accused.

Marcoleta’s plunder case: The case against the lawmaker concerns P75 million in campaign donations Marcoleta received for his 2025 senatorial run, which the Ombudsman says he failed to declare in his Statement of Contributions and Expenditures and his Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth. (READ: How Marcoleta spent P112.9 million in his 2025 election campaign)
Marcoleta has rejected the allegations against him, arguing that they had no legal basis or merit.

The lawmaker has been suspended as a senator since October 19. He has been detained since July after surrendering to authorities following the issuance of a warrant for his arrest on plunder charges filed by the Office of the Ombudsman.
Aside from plunder, Marcoleta is also facing three counts of alleged violation of Presidential Decree No. 46 (receiving gifts).
False dismissal: Rappler has debunked other false claims about the senator:

items: FACT CHECK: Supreme Court did not dismiss Marcoleta’s plunder case
FACT CHECK: Marcoleta and Estrada remain detained, contrary to claim
FACT CHECK: Marcoleta did not resign following ‘no’ vote in 2026 budget
FACT CHECK: Rodante Marcoleta is still senator

blocks.text: – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: COA questions Cebu government’s ‘heavy reliance’ on job order workers in 2025
articles.summary: COA says in its audit report that the Cebu provincial government had a total of 2,918 job order hires in 2025, or 68.24% of its total workforce that year

blocks.text: COA. The Commission on Audit in Commonwealth Avenue, Quezon City.
Rappler
COA says in its audit report that the Cebu provincial government had a total of 2,918 job order hires in 2025, or 68.24% of its total workforce that year
MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit (COA) has questioned the Cebu provincial government’s “heavy reliance” on job order (JO) workers in 2025.
COA said in its audit report that the Cebu provincial government had a total of 2,918 job order hires in 2025, or 68.24% of its total workforce of 4,276 that year.
It noted that in the same year, the Cebu government failed to fill up 1,789 vacancies in regular and casual positions.
The breakdown provided in the 2025 audit report showed the following:

items: Cebu Provincial Hospital (CPH)-Bogo City: 278 JOs vs 231 vacancies
Governor’s Office: 267 JOs vs 111 vacancies (including 67 permanent posts).
CPH-Danao City: 265 JOs vs 230 vacancies
CPH-Balamban: 257 JOs vs 228 vacancies
CPH-Carcar: 232 JOs vs 195 vacancies

blocks.text: “This heavy reliance on JO workers, despite the substantial number of unfilled regular and casual positions, indicates possible non-compliance with civil service rules and undermines the efficient utilization of government human resources,” the COA said.

The state auditor reminded the Cebu provincial government of the Local Government Code provision requiring local government units to establish organizational structures and staffing patterns based on service requirements and financial capability, subject to applicable standards prescribed by the Civil Service Commission.

The COA and the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) earlier issued Joint Circular No. 2,. s of 2020 encouraging the priority hiring of qualified JO and contract of service personnel for unfilled plantilla positions.
Based on the COA’s count, 633 nurses were hired on JO basis even if there were 371 vacant posts.

JO workers also took professional and technical positions — nursing attendants, medical specialists, medical officers, midwives, and radiologic technologists — even when there were existing vacancies for these.

“The data indicate that a substantial number of professional and technical positions essential to hospital operations are being performed by JO workers while corresponding plantilla positions remain vacant. This arrangement reflects a mismatch between the approved staffing pattern and the actual workforce composition,” state auditors said.

While LGUs are authorized to tap JO workers when justified by operational requirements and available appropriations, such engagements should only complement the existing permanent workforce, rather than serving as substitute for the number of regular employees necessary to the delivery of government services.

Auditors also noted that while JO hires do not enjoy security of employment and do not enjoy standard benefits and entitlements of employees holding plantilla positions, they are nonetheless assigned to functions involving “professional, technical, and continuing services that are more closely aligned with plantilla or COS engagements.”

COA recommended that Cebu government undertake a comprehensive review of its staffing pattern to check the necessity of getting so many JO hires, and to prioritize the hiring of qualified JO workers for vacant positions.
In their response to the audit team, Cebu provincial officials informed COA that 42% of vacant permanent positions had been published, while 47 posts had been filled — 23 from JO hires.
The Provincial Human Resource and Management Officer also reported that there were 1,013 vacant permanent positions under review as end-2025, and that 66 already filled. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Grieving families getting into debt and doing without memorials due to benefit freezes
articles.summary:
MPs to discuss bereavement support as financial help for funeral expenses and bereaved families fails to keep pace with costs

Bereaved families are borrowing money or forgoing a service with…

blocks.text: Bereaved families are borrowing money or forgoing a service with mourners because financial help available from the state no longer covers even half a typical funeral director’s fee.

“The funeral expenses payment (FSP) was originally meant to cover the cost of a simple funeral. Today, that is a pipe dream,” said Lindesay Mace, a co-manager of Down to Earth, a funeral costs support service run by the charity Quaker Social Action.

For eligible households in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Scotland has its own version), the benefit covers “reasonable” cemetery or crematorium fees plus up to £1,000 for “other funeral expenses”.

While the first element of the payment has had to keep pace with inflation, the £1,000 cap has risen once in 23 years and has been frozen since 2020, despite rising fees for the elements of a funeral that it covers.

Mace said: “Successive governments have caused the payment to devalue so much that it is failing bereaved people. We speak to people who are unable to focus on their grief due to the financial stress of having to top up the payment.”

The helpline supports about 1,000 people a year and recently assisted Carol, who was grieving the unexpected death of her daughter. She received the benefit but, despite having a “simple” funeral, says it did not cover the cost, leaving her £1,000 short. “I’m still trying to scrape together money to put a headstone on the grave,” she said.
While many of the main social security benefits are protected from losing value over time, others are not.
As well as the capped part of the FSP, the bereavement support payment (BSP) has also been frozen since its introduction in 2017. It provides short-term assistance after the death of a partner.
The freezes have “led to substantial real-terms falls in their value”, according to a recent report by the Social Security Advisory Committee.

Currently, the higher rate of bereavement support, which is available to claimants with children, comprises a £3,500 lump sum and up to 18 monthly payments of £350, totalling £9,800. Had it increased in line with the consumer prices index (CPI) it would be worth £13,448, the report says.
Meanwhile, had the £1,000 cap on funeral expenses increased in line with CPI, it would now be worth about £1,300.
after newsletter promotion

Funeral director charges have risen substantially in recent years and the cost of essentials such as mortuary care, the coffin and hearse now averages £2,605, meaning the state help meets less than 40% of this bill, the report notes.

As a result, it says, individuals “often face large shortfalls, which they must make up themselves in order for funerals to go ahead … many are forced to make difficult decisions, including selling the valuables of their deceased loved ones or turning to illegal money lenders.”

Terry Tennens, the chief executive of the National Society of Allied and Independent Funeral Directors, said: “The concern is it pushes people down the unattended cremation route because it is cheaper. There’s no memorial, and that has its consequences … when you are grieving and there’s no place to remember and gather.”
MPs will debate the BSP on Monday after a petition calling for it to be uprated annually and extended beyond 18 months received more than 108,000 signatures.

A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said the BSP was intended to provide short-term financial support. “Further help with everyday living costs may be available through benefits such as universal credit, which provide targeted, means-tested support to those in greatest need.”

items: Senator Panfilo Lacson has raised concerns about alleged double and triple appropriations for flood control projects in the proposed 2027 national budget, highlighting that some projects have already received funding in previous years.

Lacson also identified at least 30 alleged ghost multi-purpose buildings in the budget, questioning the legitimacy of funding for projects that have not been built despite receiving multiple allocations.

He criticized 'papogi spending' in the budget, which includes fragmented assistance programs, while stating he would scrutinize and seek the removal of questionable appropriations during the budget amendment process.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson has flagged alleged double and triple appropriations for some flood control projects in the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027, saying some of them had already received funding in previous years.

“Not only double, but some flood control projects even received triple budget allocations. They were funded in 2024, 2025, and 2026 but were still under the proposed budget in 2027,” Lacson told reporters on Monday, November 23.

These projects are separate from at least 30 alleged ghost multi-purpose buildings (MPBs) that the senator said he had identified in the proposed Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) budget under the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB).

Over the weekend, Lacson questioned the appropriations for 3,950 MPBs, apart from the 1,584 MPBs covered by the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF) subprogram on financial assistance to local government units (LGUs) from 2022 to 2026.

Lacson said some of the MPBs appeared to be “ghost” projects. One infrastructure project, for instance, had received appropriations from 2024 to 2026, but no structure had been built at its designated site as of this year.

“Yes, we would move for its removal. That’s the logical thing to do,” Lacson said. “Why should we approve projects with massive allocations if they are not being established? Where are our public funds going?”

An initial investigation by Lacson’s office also found that the MPB projects involved alleged commissions of up to 10%. This is lower than the 15% to 30% kickbacks previously flagged in connection with anomalous flood control projects.

blocks.caption: House pushes thousands more multi-purpose buildings. Are they really needed?

blocks.text: Lacson said he would seek the removal of questionable infrastructure projects during the period of amendments to the budget bill.

“We continue to scrutinize the bill and find more of these kinds of appropriations. If there are double appropriations, one should be removed. If there are quadruple appropriations, three should be removed,” he added.

Lacson also criticized what he called “papogi spending” — spending meant to make one look good in the eyes of the public — in the proposed budget, including MPBs and P241 billion in what he described as “fragmented ayudas.”

Lacson questioned the continued funding of several government assistance programs, including the Medical Assistance for Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients (MAIFIP), Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD), and Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS).
However, he said he would not “necessarily” seek the removal of these programs.
“They were fragmented ayuda programs. We already have 4Ps, UniFAST, and tertiary education law,” Lacson said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Some flood control items in 2027 budget funded twice, says Lacson
articles.summary: Sen. Ping Lacson said his staff has found flood control items with "double appropriations" in the P7.2-trillion spending bill, which will be up for plenary debate at the Senate this week.

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 2:51pm

MANILA, Philippines — Flood control projects are back in the national budget, and with them an old problem in public works spending: duplicate and overlapping appropriations, a senator flagged on Monday, November 23.
Sen. Ping Lacson said his staff has found flood control items with "double appropriations" in the P7.2-trillion spending bill, which will be up for plenary debate at the Senate this week.
Lacson said he would move to delete the extra entries during the Senate's period of amendments and, if needed, at the bicameral conference committee.

"Meron pa rin kaming nasilip. Double appropriations. Flood control na nga, doble pa yung appropriations," Lacson said in an interview with DZMM. (We found something else: double appropriations. It's flood control, of all things, and the funding is doubled.)
His claim adds to a growing list of warnings about the 2027 budget since the start of the legislative budget season.

Civil society coalitions, business groups and senators, including Lacson, have raised concerns over lump-sum allocations, duplicate and nearly identical entries, and thousands of projects allegedly added by the House without publicly available supporting documents.

The same irregular items have previously been flagged in the 2023 to 2025 budgets, some of which were later found to be funding ghost and substandard flood control works. A joint statement by business groups in late October warned the public has "already paid dearly for this practice" and that the 2027 "must not repeat that history."

In August, the Department of Public Works and Highways, then led by Secretary Vince Dizon, said it had cut its 2027 project list to 11,395 from the usual 20,000 or more, as part of reforms to prevent "duplicate and overlapping projects."
However, Lacson said such items are still carried in the proposed 2027 budget.
The DPWH for 2027 is seeking at least P107.4 billion for flood control works, the lowest allocation for the program since 2019.

In 2025, the DPWH slashed P252 billion from its proposed 2026 budget after investigations revealed the department had long funded substandard flood mitigation structures, duplicated existing allocations, and masked non-existent "ghost" projects.
Lacson's latest claim comes after a separate allegation he made over the weekend: that there are 30 non-existing multi-purpose buildings parked in the proposed 2027 budget.

"We have taken drone shots of at least one ‘ghost multi-purpose building’ that received numerous fund allocations in 2024, 2025, 2026 and is being included again for funding under the 2027 budget measure," Lacson said in a statement Sunday, November 22.

Citing initial findings, Lacson said MPBs also carry "commissions" of up to 10%. That is lower than the 15 to 30% in kickbacks he said earlier this year went to proponents of anomalous flood control projects.

There are at least 3,950 multi-purpose buildings in the Senate version of the bill, on top of another 1,584 covered by the Local Government Support Fund's financial assistance subprogram for local governments, Lacson said.

Earlier, the People's Budget Coalition, an alliance of more than 40 civil society groups, said the House more than doubled funding of the multi-purpose buildings to P83.7 billion from P41 billion in the executive proposal.

House members defended the increase, including Rep. Terry Ridon (Bicol Saro), co-chair of the House infrastructure committee, who argued the amount reflected public need and covers facilities such as senior citizens' centers.

articles.title: Monday briefing: What could Andy Burnham’s reset mean for the UK?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The prime minister has reopened the debate over a future relationship with a changed EU – as the bloc faces the rise of the far right, a protectionist economic agenda and…

blocks.text: Good morning. Nobody really wants to think about Brexit any more, save for the original Brexiters, who seem delighted that Andy Burnham’s “reset” with the EU has given them an excuse to get the old gang back together. But arguments about whether the UK should rejoin the EU will reignite in parliament this week, as Burnham briefs MPs on the deal he agreed on Friday.

That deal wasn’t so much a victory as the culmination of Keir Starmer’s incrementalist approach to UK-EU relations. Its core agreements haven’t been ratified by member states yet, and the EU won’t sign them off until Britain resolves a dispute over tuition fees for European students. Burnham is apparently “determined” to take the UK back into the EU, but don’t expect any progress on that before the next general election.

Putting aside the question of whether a second referendum would merely reopen old wounds, Europe has changed dramatically since 2016, creating new challenges for any government seeking a closer relationship with the EU. For this morning’s newsletter, I discussed these challenges and what they mean for rejoining with Mujtaba Rahman, managing director for Europe at the Eurasia Group and a frequent contributor to the Guardian’s Opinion section. That’s after the headlines.
Weekend roundup

items: Cop31 | The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal that “failed to meet the moment” in a dramatic finish to the UN talks in Turkey. The proposed deal failed to endorse a away from fossil fuels that more than 130 countries demanded.
Russia | A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

Weapons| The Red Cross and other rights groups have warned that it will soon be too late to properly regulate the development of autonomous weapons. The warning came as the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons concluded without an agreement on an instrument for regulating autonomous weapons.

UK news | Dozens of hospitals are so short of money they may not be able to continue caring for patients and are being forced to make “unpalatable” cuts to services and staff, the Guardian can reveal.

West Bank | Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank after dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday.

blocks.text: In depth: The EU has changed. What does that mean for Burnham’s ambitions?

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham has said all options are ‘on the table’. Photograph: Hannah McKay/PA

blocks.text: Three separate deals were announced at Friday’s summit in Brussels: one on food and drink, another on emissions trading, and a third on youth mobility, which will allow British students to work, live, study and travel in the EU and give reciprocal access to EU students in Britain (for a full recap, read Jennifer Rankin and Alexandra Topping’s explainer). Burnham wants to go further, and both he and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, have used the near-identical phrase that all options are “on the table” for Britain’s future relationship with the EU.

You’d be forgiven for feeling weary about revisiting the last decade in British politics. As one Labour MP recently told the Financial Times (£), “nobody is asking for this.” Burnham seems to be testing the ground ahead of a general election, hoping that a campaign to rejoin, or at least move closer to, the EU could plausibly win over progressive defectors.

Still, Friday’s agreement was a reminder of how difficult it is to negotiate with a club of 27. Member states, including France and Italy, issued a statement making it clear that the deal wouldn’t be implemented unless Burnham offered a deal on tuition fees for EU students at British universities. “There’s a fairly strong sense that we’ve reached the end of the incremental style of negotiating,” Mujtaba Rahman tells me. “There isn’t much more for the UK to do before it starts to resemble a cherrypicking state.” And there are other developments that will be on the minds of negotiators and ministers contemplating the UK’s future relationship with Europe.
Has the far right made the idea of European Union membership less attractive?

This is one of the major developments: Europe has become decidedly more right-wing since 2016. Though the European far right lost one of its key figureheads when Viktor Orbán was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, far-right parties govern in the Czech Republic and Italy, and support for them is rising in Austria and Germany. The proportion of voters in Europe who cast their ballots for far-right parties has grown more than five times since the 1990s, and has increased particularly sharply over the last three years.

Whether this will make rejoining less appealing depends largely on what happens next year in the French elections. Marine Le Pen, who is now favoured to win, wants to slash France’s contribution to the EU budget and drastically downsize the union. It’s possible that a Le Pen presidency could embolden other EU member states to seek closer ties with a pro-European British government, but it’s also possible that Le Pen’s domestic policies, such as reducing the retirement age to 60, could trigger a domestic economic crisis and inflame a conflict between the EU and France, one of its founding member states. “If Marine Le Pen wins, and France tries to enforce a domestic programme that runs in opposition to the EU, then I think a lot of people in the UK will look at the resulting crisis and think, ‘Thank God we’re out of that’,” Mujtaba says.
Is the EU’s new protectionism a reason to rejoin?

The EU’s Made in Europe strategy would have been almost unimaginable a decade ago, when progressives criticised the union for enforcing free-market globalisation on its members and forbidding state aid. The strategy, which uses public money to support goods made by companies in the single market, is a sign of both how isolated the UK has become and how much the world has changed. Burnham is now trying to make “reindustrialisation” part of his agenda at home, but the EU’s initiative is designed to disadvantage countries outside the EU. It risks scuppering his efforts by deindustrialising the UK car industry, which relies on European buyers.

“It’s very hard for the government to influence this because the Made in Europe negotiations are internal to the EU. And it’s very hard for member states to provide any guarantees because there’s no UK guardian at the table,” Mujtaba says. The EU hasn’t included the UK in the scheme, though Friday’s summit promised closer cooperation on steel and electric vehicle supply chains. But that may require the UK to follow EU policies without having any ability to shape them, making the idea of full membership much more appealing.
Would rejoining mean taking a different approach to defence?

This is perhaps the strongest reason of all for rejoining, but it’s also another area where the EU’s approach has evolved significantly over the last decade. “The geopolitical environment is forcing the EU to do a bunch of things the UK has historically taken issue with,” Mujtaba says. “It’s intervening in areas of policy that would have traditionally been the purview of nation states.” In particular, the EU’s Security Action for Europe facility (Safe), a new EU defence fund offering up to €150bn in loans to member states to fund defence investments, shifts defence from a national concern to one of wider European governance.

Britain refused to pay the financial contribution that Brussels wanted for it to participate in the Safe fund, though there are signs that the two sides may still reach a deal. But any campaign to rejoin would need to critically evaluate the deep ties and so-called “special relationship” between the UK and US in light of an EU that has grown to regard the US as an unreliable partner on security.

“The UK isn’t quite as far-reaching in its conclusions about the US,” Mujtaba says. “You don’t hear UK officials talking about the Americans in the same way that European officials are talking about the Americans.”

articles.title: Is rule-breaking contagious? The bad apple effect explained
articles.summary: Seeing someone break a rule makes people more likely to break it too, a new study finds, especially when the rule-breaker is on their side politically. Watching others behave well barely made a…

image.caption: Image: Guo Lei/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

A new study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group."
How was the study done, and what are its limits?

The researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.
Internet addiction: When life is only online
Is rule-breaking contagious?

Rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.
Small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.
Most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.
Do good role models make people follow rules?
Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.
People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.
Are people more likely to break rules when their own side does?
People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.
Can a few bad apples spoil the whole group?
To see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.
What does this mean in real life?
Molleman calls the work fundamental science and says the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

He also says it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing."
This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

articles.title: Maguindanao massacre victims' kin urge CA to resolve pending appeals
articles.summary: Families of the Maguindanao massacre victims on Monday renewed their appeal to the Court of Appeals (CA) to resolve pending appeals in the 2009 case, including those involving civil damages and the…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 2:09pm

Families of the Maguindanao massacre victims on Monday renewed their appeal to the Court of Appeals (CA) to resolve pending appeals in the 2009 case, including those involving civil damages and the legal recognition of photojournalist Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay as the 58th victim.
Lawyer Gilbert Andres, executive director of the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) Philippines, filed an 11-page second motion for resolution before the CA on behalf of 19 families.

“Seventeen years na po silang naghihintay, ‘yung iba po ay namatay na po, ‘yung iba po ay naghihintay na sa kanilang mga beds, ‘yung iba po ay may mga sakit na po kaya hindi po sila namin kasama,” Andres told reporters.
(They have been waiting for 17 years. Some have already passed away, others are bedridden, and some are ill, which is why they could not join us today.)
“Kaya sila po ay nagsusumamo at talagang nanghihingi sa ating kagalang-galang na Court office na talagang agaran na po desisyunan lahat po ng pending appeals sa Court of Appeals,” he added.
(That is why they are appealing and earnestly asking the honorable court to immediately decide on all pending appeals before the Court of Appeals.)
The motion was filed on the 17th anniversary of the Nov. 23, 2009 massacre, the deadliest election-related violence in Philippine history.
The attack also remains the deadliest single incident targeting journalists worldwide, with 32 journalists and media workers among the 58 people killed.
The victims’ families also renewed their appeal for Momay to be officially recognized as the 58th victim of the massacre.
The Quezon City Regional Trial Court had acquitted the accused of Momay’s murder and dismissed his family's claim for civil damages.
Momay’s body was never recovered. The only physical evidence linked to him found at the crime scene was a set of dentures.
Earlier on Monday, Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda urged the CA to resolve the pending appeals in the case, saying justice should not be delayed further after 17 years.

“I therefore urge the Court of Appeals to resolve the pending appeals with dispatch, consistent with due process and rights of all parties. Let us ensure that justice is not delayed any further,” Zalameda said.
Andres welcomed the chief justice’s call, saying it reinforced the families’ appeal for the CA to act on the long-pending cases.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Burnham not ‘backtracking’ on creating closer links with EU, officials say
articles.summary:
Government wants to let trade deal ‘breathe a bit’, insiders say, after speculation No 10 is dialling back ambitions

Andy Burnham is not backtracking or delaying his ambitions to create even…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is not backtracking or delaying his ambitions to create even closer links with the EU in the wake of a landmark summit in Brussels, the Guardian has been told, after signs of an apparent slowdown in the timetable.

The prime minister has promised to set out options for the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU, including the possibility of rejoining, saying last week that these would be outlined later in the year.

But speaking at Friday’s UK-EU summit after finalising a deal on reducing food and drink checks, emissions trading and a mutual youth mobility scheme, Burnham talked instead about “brainstorming” ideas with the EU for what comes next, with a timetable given of some months.

The apparent slowdown prompted speculation No 10 wants to dial back the political pressure and prevent his agenda being swamped by arguments about the EU, with campaign groups being formed before a possible debate about rejoining.

But after Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, talked warmly on Sunday about the benefits of more integration, government officials said this was still the aim after a “really positive” summit in which the EU side, they said, promised to be as helpful as possible with whatever comes next.
“There is no backtracking or pumping the brakes,” one said. “The government just wants to let this deal breathe a bit, and point to the benefits.”
Another official said: “There hasn’t been a timetable shift since the summit. It’s being considered alongside the domestic agenda and the 10-year plan.”

Burnham will seek to keep up the initiative from the summit with a visit on Monday to a branch of Morrisons, in part to see the supermarket chain’s efforts in employing young people, but also to push home his message that the deal on food checks will lower retail prices.
Also on Monday the prime minister is expected to brief the Commons on the summit and deal, where he will face a hostile reception from opposition parties, particularly Reform UK.

In a speech to the CBI conference on Monday, Nigel Farage, the Reform leader, will tell business leaders that rejoining the EU would be “a disaster” for the UK economy, and that his party would reverse the deal made in Brussels.

Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, has been critical of Burnham’s negotiations, but noticeably less trenchant about the wider idea of smoothing trade links with Europe, part of a strategy to focus instead on subjects such as the economy and defence.

“Seamless trade benefits the UK, but it also benefits the EU,” she will say, according to an advance extract of her own speech to the CBI conference. “If we can make our trading relationship better, good. I’m all for working on a smarter deal.”

In contrast, Theresa May, who carried out the bulk of the Brexit negotiations with Brussels before being replaced by Boris Johnson, made a rare intervention on day-to-day politics to warn Burnham that rejoining would tie up his government for years.
She told the BBC: “That’s one of the reasons why I looked slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham was talking about – further negotiations of going into the EU.

“As a country, we voted for Brexit. When I was prime minister, I was very clear: we should deliver on that vote. So I’m afraid my message to him really is: people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on.”
In his own interview with the BBC on Sunday, Miliband argued that closer links with the EU would mean the UK having a say on decisions made by Brussels.

“At the moment, what the situation is is that we are essentially rule takers,” the foreign secretary said. “Businesses are rule takers if they want to sell into the European market. So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union, but at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms.”
He said this was “the worst of all worlds” and it meant there was a clear case to integrate more closely into EU markets.

Another reason for even closer ties, he said, was the transformed geopolitical order since 2016, including Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the US’s distancing from Europe under Donald Trump.

articles.title: MPs urge Miliband to force UK overseas territories to publish public company registers
articles.summary:
Improvements in corporate transparency ‘essential’ amid ‘outright disregard for the will of parliament’, says cross-party group

Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force…

blocks.text: Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency.

Ahead of a meeting between the foreign secretary and overseas territories this week, a cross-party group of MPs from Labour, the Tories, Lib Dems and Greens wrote to Miliband calling on him to mandate public registers of beneficial ownership of companies.

The group, coordinated by the all-party group on anti-corruption (APPG), said an improvement in corporate transparency in the overseas territories was essential after “years of broken promises and missed deadlines from certain jurisdictions, and despite repeated commitments to ending secrecy”.
They said some territories such as Gibraltar, Montserrat and St Helena had successfully opened corporate registers to the public.

But they called out the British Virgin Islands, saying it “in particular continues to let the British family down”. They said the Cayman Islands has raised its search fees to “prohibitive levels”, and Turks and Caicos have introduced huge fines for disclosing information from the register which they said was “undermining the entire purpose of open registers”.
They said that persistent engagement in good faith from the UK government has yielded few results, in the face of “outright disregard for the will of parliament”.

The BVI has a register launched this year which allows people to apply for access to ownership information if they have a “legitimate interest” such as investigating money laundering. A BVI Government spokesperson said: “We are proud of the BVI’s Legitimate Interest Access register introduced earlier this year, which allows for prompt, proportionate access, in line with international standards.

“We continue to work closely with the UK Government, delivering a major governance and regulatory reform programme to support global efforts combatting illicit finance, enforcing sanctions and recovering criminal assets - with significant progress recently recognised by the Financial Action Task Force.”

However, ahead of the meeting, the MPs including former Conservative Foreign Office minister Andrew Mitchell and Labour anti-corruption expert Phil Brickell are asking Miliband to lay an order in council mandating fully public registers of beneficial ownership in jurisdictions that continue to fail to meet their obligations.

They said it was important for UK national security “because continued secrecy undermines our ability to enforce sanctions and leaves us open to hostile state actors and criminal networks”. Second, they said developing countries continue to be destabilised and looted by kleptocrats using Britain’s own offshore financial centres to clean and stash their ill-gotten gains.

Parliament voted for open registers in 2018 and the UK government had expected public access registers to be in place in all overseas territories and crown dependencies by 2023. However, this deadline was not met.

While an order in council to mandate open registers was drafted in 2020, the government said that because there were “firm commitments” from the overseas territories to introduce public registers, the order would not be used. It said it would keep this decision under review.
after newsletter promotion

Brickell, Labour chair of the APPG, said “it should never have come to this but every year of deliberate delay is another year in which kleptocrats, tax dodgers and money launderers can hide behind a British flag”.
“That is a stain on the reputation of our global family. This joint ministerial council must be the moment we finally draw a line under it.”

Mitchell, a Conservative vice-chair of the APPG and former development secretary, said: “When parliament voted for public registers in 2018, it was not making a polite request. It was the clear, cross-party will of the House of Commons, and it should have been respected.

“Instead, money stolen from some of the poorest people on earth is still being hidden behind anonymous companies in British jurisdictions. That money should be building hospitals and schools. It is paying for yachts and mansions instead, and the price is measured in lives. The British family has been patient for long enough. The foreign secretary has the power to act, and I urge him to use it.”

A Foreign Office spokesperson said: “Security is the first duty of any government. Hostile states and malign actors can exploit opaque corporate structures like those in the British Virgin Islands to hide their assets and support activity that threatens our national security.

“Ministers are actively considering how best to ensure that, where the risks are greatest, law enforcement agencies have the information they need to progress critical investigations. We will continue ongoing engagement with Overseas Territories on these issues.”

articles.title: Chief justice to CA: Resolve pending appeals in Ampatuan massacre now
articles.summary: During the Supreme Court’s Flag Ceremony on Monday, November 23, Zalameda called on the appellate court to “resolve the pending appeals with dispatch.”

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 1:44pm
Police investigators look for evidence next to a backhoe after a vehicle and human remains were dug up from a shallow grave in the town of Ampatuan, Maguindanao in a Nov. 25, 2009 file photo.
AFP, File
MANILA, Philippines — Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda has urged the Court of Appeals to resolve the ongoing appeals related to the Ampatuan massacre.
Speaking at the Supreme Court’s flag ceremony on Monday, November 23 — the 17th anniversary of the killings — Zalameda urged the appellate court to “resolve the pending appeals with dispatch.”
“As we speak of protecting those who stand for justice, we must also remember the victims of the Ampatuan Massacre, whose 17th anniversary we commemorate today,” Zalameda said.

“The victims and their families have waited long enough. I therefore urge the Court of Appeals to resolve the pending appeals with dispatch, consistent with due process and rights of all parties. Let us ensure that justice is not delayed any further,” he added.
Meanwhile, the Center for International Law has filed an urgent motion before the Court of Appeals seeking the immediate resolution of pending appeals in the Ampatuan massacre cases.
The motion also reiterates the call for judicial recognition of Reynaldo “Bebot” Momay as the 58th victim of the massacre.

Background on the case. The tragedy, also named the Maguindanao massacre, took place on Nov. 23, 2009, leaving 58 people dead — including 32 journalists — as they traveled to file the certificate of candidacy of Esmael Mangudadatu.
On Dec. 19, 2019, Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 221 convicted the Ampatuan brothers of 57 counts of murder and sentenced them to reclusion perpetua without parole.

Twenty-eight co-accused, including police officers, were convicted of 57 counts of murder and sentenced to 40 years in prison, while 15 others were sentenced to six to 10 years as accessories. Fifty-five individuals, including Datu Sajid Islam Ampatuan, were acquitted.

articles.title: SILG Remulla on hunt for Zaldy, Bato, Atong, Bantag: Good results will come soon
articles.summary: Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Monday said authorities are continuing operations to locate and arrest high-profile fugitives, expressing hope that there would be…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 1:41pm

Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Monday said authorities are continuing operations to locate and arrest high-profile fugitives, expressing hope that there would be developments before the end of the year.

"Well, we're at it. The operations continue. Makakaasa kayo (Rest assured) that good results will come soon," Remulla told reporters in an ambush interview when asked for updates on the government's efforts to track down the fugitives.
Asked whether authorities could make progress before the year ends, Remulla replied, "Sana (Hopefully)."

Among the high-profile fugitives being pursued by authorities are former lawmaker Zaldy Co, Senator Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, businessman Charlie "Atong" Ang, and former Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) chief Gerald Bantag.

The Office of the Ombudsman has charged Co and several former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials over alleged irregularities in a P289-million road dike project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro.

Dela Rosa is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the crimes against humanity case stemming from former president Rodrigo Duterte's war on drugs. The senator, who was the Philippine National Police chief during Duterte's term as president, is accused of being a co-perpetrator in the alleged crimes.
A P50-million reward is being offered for information that would lead to the senator's arrest.

Authorities are also searching for Ang, who remains the only accused still at large in connection with the missing sabungeros case. Arrest warrants have been issued against Ang and other accused over multiple counts of kidnapping with homicide and kidnapping and serious illegal detention.
A P10-million reward is offered for information on Ang's whereabouts.
Bantag, meanwhile, is wanted in connection with the death of Jun Villamor, the alleged middleman in the October 2022 killing of broadcaster Percy Lapid.
A Muntinlupa Regional Trial Court ordered Bantag's arrest in April 2023.
A P2-million reward is also offered for information that would lead to Bantag's arrest. —KG, GMA News
