articles.title: MANIBELA's 2-day transport strike starts
articles.summary: Transport group Samahang Manibela, Mananakay at Nagkaisang Terminal ng Transportasyon (MANIBELA) on Monday began its two-day transport strike to protest the reported replacement of Land…

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 8:09am

Transport group Samahang Manibela, Mananakay at Nagkaisang Terminal ng Transportasyon (MANIBELA) on Monday began its two-day transport strike to protest the reported replacement of Land Transportation Office (LTO) chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao.
Interviewed on Super Radyo dzBB, MANIBELA national president Mar Valbuena said the group wants Lacanilao to remain in his post to continue the reforms he has implemented at the agency.

“Panglima na ata itong pagpapalit na ito sa hepe ng LTO at sa haba ng panahon, ang haba namin sa kalsada, ngayon lang kami nakaranas ng medyo patas na laban sa pamumuno ni Asec. Markus Lacanilao,” Valbuena said.

(This is probably the fifth time that the LTO chief has been replaced, and in all the time we've been on the road, we've only experienced a fairly fair fight under the leadership of Asec. Markus Lacanilao.)
Valbuena recognized Lacanilao for improving the processing of vehicle registration renewals and driver's licenses, as well as disciplining LTO personnel including those assigned to regional offices.
He claimed that personnel previously removed from the agency over alleged corruption could be reinstated under the planned leadership change.
The reported replacement is Atty. Noreen Bernadette San Luis, according to Valbuena. He said he had heard that President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. had already signed her appointment.
MANIBELA had been discussing the possible leadership change for nearly a month.
Vabuena lamented that transport groups were not consulted or informed about the planned change, despite their concerns.
MANIBELA said the strike could extend to three days depending on the sentiments of the transport sector.
The group planned to march from Agham Road to the LTO headquarters along East Avenue in Quezon City starting at 7 a.m. on Monday, according to a report on GMA News’ Unang Balita.
Meanwhile, the Department of Transportation (DOTr) said there was no official announcement yet from the Office of the President regarding a change in LTO leadership.
The DOTr arranged free rides from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. along several routes:

items: Quiapo -Cubao
Quiapo - Doña Carmen, Commonwealth
Quiapo - Fairview
Taft (Buendia) - Alabang
Commonwealth - Cubao (East Avenue and V. Luna)

blocks.text: Also, the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) will offer free rides to assist commuters affected by the strike.

The NCRPO also placed around 6,000 police personnel on alert for the two-day protest, while the Quezon City Police District advised commuters to monitor traffic advisories and report emergencies or incidents requiring police assistance.
—Joviland Rita/KG, GMA News

articles.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.summary: AI employees in the industry's epicentre - San Francisco - worry that the sector is overheated.

blocks.text: Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".
Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.
"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.
Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.
"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.
All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.title: Lacson challenges Marcos' Iran reason for economic slowdown
articles.summary: The Iran war hit the whole ASEAN. But Lacson asks, why did Philippine growth fall further?

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 7:30am
Composite image shows Sen. Ping Lacson at a Senate hearing on Oct. 23, 2026 and President Bongbong Marcos at an ASEAN event on Nov. 17, 2026.
Lacson office; ASEAN PH; Philstar.com composite

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Ping Lacson rejected President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s attempt to trace the Philippines' economic difficulties entirely to the Iran conflict, pointing to faster growth in other Southeast Asian countries.

"With all due respect Mr. President, blaming the US-Iran conflict will not suffice. Our ASEAN neighbors face the same oil-price pressures, yet Vietnam's GDP rises to 9.95%, Indonesia is steady at 5.47%, Singapore and Malaysia with 5.4% and 5.3% respectively," Lacson said Sunday, November 22.
The Philippine economy, in comparison, grew by 2.1% in the third quarter, slowing from 2.4% in the previous three months, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority.
Lacson was responding to Marcos' defense of his economic managers after the senator urged the administration to reassess their performance.
"All the difficulties we're going through can be clearly directly traced to the war in Iran," Marcos said November 20 at a press conference in Shenzhen, China.

The senator said, however, he wasn't seeking a change in the Cabinet's composition. His call, he said, was for the administration to reconsider the policies behind an economy that is slowing more sharply than those of several regional peers.
"Our growth is lowest at 2.1% and still decelerating. I did not posit a cabinet reshuffle, but a long hard look at our economic team to revisit some of our economic policies," he added.

The country's economic weaknesses extended beyond what is directly attributed to oil prices. Agriculture, forestry and fishing contracted by 4.8%, while industry was virtually flat. Gross capital formation, a measure of investment, declined by 0.2%.
Household consumption, traditionally the economy's main engine, grew by only 2.4%.
More than an external shock. The Iran conflict has nevertheless inflicted visible economic damage by raising energy and transport costs.

Headline inflation accelerated to a three-year high of 7.8% in October from 7.2% in September. Transport prices rose 20.1% from a year earlier, while housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels increased by 9.3%.
But the administration's own economic planners have identified a broader set of pressures.
In July, the Development Budget Coordination Committee cited governance-related concerns and weaker business and consumer confidence alongside geopolitical tensions.
It also warned that high inflation could restrain consumption and investment, while slower remittances, weaker visitor arrivals and El Niño could further depress growth.
The DBCC cut its 2026 growth projection to between 3.5% and 4.5%, reflecting both domestic and external risks.

articles.title: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'
articles.summary: The prime minister will tell MPs the deal agreed on Friday is a "choice between a broken status quo or change".

blocks.text: The prime minister will tell Parliament on Monday the "landmark" deal struck with the EU means there is a "very real prospect" the next decade can be "much better" than the last one.
The deal is a "choice between a broken status quo or change", Andy Burnham will tell MPs.
He will also call it "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament" - repeating his claim it could add £17bn to the British economy.

The PM described it on Friday as a "win-win" deal with the EU on British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. But since then a host of politicians have criticised the plan, with one former prime minister urging him to "move on" from Brexit.
Burnham believes the agreement reached in Brussels "holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a much better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through".
"The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands and I believe we should take it," he will say in his speech.
He will also paint the move as a choice "between easing pressure on the cost of living or allowing food prices to rise further" and "creating opportunities for young people or denying them".
He believes polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
But his announcement on Friday was greeted with a chorus of criticism from a number of opposing political figures.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was unfair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels.
She questioned the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
Badenoch accused him of having "plucked that figure out of the air" before saying "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Meanwhile Reform UK leader Farage called the deal a "very good day for the EU", before adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added in a social media post: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Over the weekend former prime ministers including Theresa May, Sir Tony Blair and Rishi Sunak also criticised the EU-UK deal.
May, who presided over three years of Brexit negotiations during her premiership, said she was "aghast" by the deal and warned Andy Burnham should "move on".
Sir Tony, who was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told The Sunday Times Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms, and allows more innovation on technology.
Badenoch will use her speech at the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) annual conference on Monday to criticise Burnham's EU deal.
She will accuse the prime minister of securing a "terrible" deal and will say he should be "aiming a lot higher" in terms of driving growth.
Farage will tell the same conference that establishing closer ties with the EU would be a "disaster" for British businesses.
Rejoining the EU will hit the small firms that do not even trade with Europe with more red tape, more compliance costs, more Brussels rules they never asked for, he is expected to say.
On Friday, the PM said that over the coming months both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for the UK's "long-term relationship" with the EU.
He was also clear that the deal he struck was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it".
He added: "But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

articles.title: 2-time Cy Young winner Skubal agrees to record 9-year, $450M US deal with Mets: reports
articles.summary: Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was the top free agent on this offseason's market, has a agreed to record $450 million US, nine-year contract with the New York Mets, a person…

image.caption: The New York Mets and ace pitcher Tarik Skubal have agreed to a record-setting 9-year, $450M US deal on Sunday, according to multiple reports. (Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)

blocks.text: MLB

Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was the top free agent on this offseason's market, has a agreed to record $450 million US, nine-year contract with the New York Mets, a person familiar the negotiations told The Associated Press on Sunday.
Blue Jays were reportedly among teams who met with 30-year-old ace

Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young Award winner who was this offseason's top free agent, has agreed to a record $450 million US, nine-year contract with the New York Mets, a person familiar with the negotiations told The Associated Press on Sunday.
The person spoke on condition of anonymity because the agreement was subject to a successful physical.

Skubal's deal, averaging $50 million annually, is the largest for a pitcher, topping Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million, 12-year contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers that started in 2024. The previous high for a pitcher's average annual value was $43.33 million for Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander.
It's the fourth largest deal among all baseball players, trailing Juan Soto's $765 million, Shohei Ohtani's $700 million and Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s $500 million.
The Toronto Blue Jays were among multiple teams reported to have met with Skubal prior to agreeing to join the Mets.

Skubal's agreement includes a full no-trade clause and a $45 million signing bonus that is shielded from the management lockout that threatens the 2027 season, the person said. It includes $30 million in deferred payments from 2036-45.

He joins a Mets team that finished last in the NL East at 74-88 despite owner Steve Cohen bankrolling baseball's highest payroll on opening day at roughly $352 million. New York's starters had a 4.47 ERA, ranking 23rd in the majors. Skubal will top a rotation featuring youngsters Nolan McLean and Christian Scott, with veterans Sean Manaea and Kodai Senga also under contract.

Skubal had plans to meet with at least six teams this month, including the Mets, Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres. His deal comes about a week before MLB owners are expected to lock out the players in a labor fight centreing on management's push for a salary cap. MLB has proposed a hard cap of $258.2 million for 2028. Skubal and Soto alone would account for nearly 40 per cent of that cap.
A two-time All-Star left-hander who turned 30 on Nov. 20, Skubal is 43-17 with a 2.42 ERA in 88 starts over the last four seasons, striking out 655 and walking 95 in 546 innings.
Skubal had a $32 million salary this year after winning a record amount in salary arbitration.

items: Skubal to Dodgers, Peralta to Rays as MLB teams add pitching at trade deadline
Tigers pitcher Tarik Skubal to have elbow surgery to remove loose bodies

blocks.text: Skubal was 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts this year for Detroit and the Los Angeles Dodgers, who acquired him on Aug. 2 for three prospects: right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith, and outfielder Zyhir Hope. Skubal didn't pitch for the Tigers between April 29 and June 13 because of surgery to remove a loose body in his pitching elbow. Dodgers head team physician Dr. Neal ElAttrache used a NanoNeedle scope 2.0 to perform the procedure, designed to speed recovery.

Skubal was 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA in a pair of postseason starts for the Dodgers. He beat Atlanta in a Division Series opener and lost Game 1 of the NL League Championship Series against Milwaukee, allowing two runs over five innings in a 2-1 defeat. The Brewers went on to sweep the two-time defending World Series champions.

He averaged 96.8 mph with his four-seam fastball this year, down from 97.6 mph in 2025, when he won his second straight AL Cy Young Award. He threw 38 per cent four-seamers this year, 25.6 per cent changeups, 17.5 per cent sinkers, 13.9 per cent sliders and 5 per cent curveballs.
Skubal is 66-44 with a 3.02 ERA in 160 starts and three relief appearances over seven major league seasons with 1,075 strikeouts over 925 1/3 innings.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ US healthcare proposal
articles.summary:
Democratic senator-elect reiterates suggestion to rename Medicare for All after Trump if president allows bill to pass

Michigan US senator-elect

blocks.text: Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage.
“If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”

El-Sayed made those remarks on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press, where he reiterated his pledge to pursue a single-payer, national healthcare program after the Democrat became the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate during the midterms earlier in November.

Trump’s Republican party is going to lose control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency. But the president has made clear his intention to wield his legislative veto powers whenever he sees fit.
Appearing on Sunday’s Meet the Press, El-Sayed said he would not mind Medicare for All – a big part of his campaign platform – being named “TrumpCare” as long as such a program came into existence.

“I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country. And if the president is serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card,” El-Sayed said to Meet the Press host Kristen Welker, making a double entendre for a term that – when the T is lowercase – also refers to a card that beats out others in card games.

El-Sayed told Welker that such a Trump card would be in effect “from the moment [people] are born to the moment that they pass away – that guarantees them the healthcare that has been so elusive in this country without premiums, co-pays and deductibles”.

The senator-elect’s comments come after he previously suggested to CNN that he is not above stroking Trump’s prodigious ego to get legislation passed – including by naming Medicare for All “TrumpCare”.

He also previously wrote on social media, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “TrumpCare” inscribed on it: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”
Trump has spent much of his second presidency trying to get as much as possible named after him – from institutions, physical buildings and currency.
El-Sayed also said that he supports healthcare reform proposed by Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator.
Sanders’ proposal would create a single-payer system in which the federal government insures everybody, financed by an increase in taxes, while eliminating private insurance.

But El-Sayed said he is not focused on eliminating private insurance as an option, which Sanders aims to eliminate by having everything primary and preventive services to hospital stays covered under his proposed plan. Out-of-pocket costs on deductibles and co-pays – staples of the rapacious private insurance industry to which most Americans must resort – would also be eliminated under Sanders’ plan.
El-Sayed said he wants to “provide you basic public health insurance no matter who you are in this country” while being open to the idea of not taking alternative options away.

The senator-elect said he has a meeting on the books with JD Vance. El-Sayed would not share the agenda of the meeting, but he confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff contacted him after his election victory.

articles.title: Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets
articles.summary: Protesters gathered in Istanbul to show their support for press freedom in Turkey. The protest was called just days after the police raided Sozcu TV and arrested several senior staff members.

image.caption: Protesters' placards read in Turkish: "No to trustee takeovers!" and "Where did all those truckloads of money go?"Image: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Several thousand people in Istanbul took to the streets on Sunday to protest the closure of several opposition-linked media outlets in Turkey.
Protesters chanted, cheered, and whistled as they marched several kilometers through the city, calling for press freedom and freedom of expression.

They carried a huge banner that read: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press, and freedom for journalists." The protesters were also carrying placards that read, "The press cannot be silenced."

blocks.caption: Protesters held up copies of the opposition newspaper SozcuImage: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What sparked the protests?
Turkey's main opposition party, Yeni Parti, called for a protest just days after police raided Sozcu TV, one of the last opposition-aligned television channels.
Senior staff members were arrested during the raid. A government-appointed trustee was installed, and the TV company was placed under compulsory administration.
It was the third takeover in a year following similar actions against Tele1, Halk TV, Turkey's most-watched news channel, and the leading digital news website, T24.
Timur Soykan, a journalist who was briefly detained for criticizing the government, said that the government was doing everything in its power to silence journalists but was failing to do so.
Soykan asked the public to support Halk TV journalists, who plan to continue broadcasting on a new YouTube channel.
Increasing crackdown on critical media in Turkey
Over the past decade, press freedom has faced sustained pressure in the form of prosecutions, digital censorship, and government accusations that journalists are spreading "fake news."

In the last two months alone, Turkey has arrested several journalists for their reporting on a multibillion-dollar investment fund scandal. At least two of the journalists remain in pretrial detention.
According to the media rights group MLSA, twenty-five journalists are currently imprisoned in Turkey.
This year, Reporters Without Borders ranked Turkey 163rd out of 180 countries in its Press Freedom Index.

articles.title: US intelligence chief says he trusts Trump’s description of Putin as ‘my friend’
articles.summary:
Jay Clayton was pressed on Trump’s characterization of Putin during media appearances on Sunday

Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump…

blocks.text: Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.

Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”
On CNN’s State of the Union, Dana Bash asked Clayton whether he also thinks Putin is a friend to the US.

“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen,” said Clayton on Sunday. “Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable and, in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”
Bash pressed on whether Clayton personally agrees that Putin should be considered a friend.
“Dana, in different contexts, you can use different words. The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable,” Clayton replied.
Speaking with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on This Week, Clayton made similar comments, saying that “using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate” in the context of the summit.

“That conversation, that picture – historic, historic picture – was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton said on Sunday, referring to Trump’s post. “In that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate.”
Clayton also dodged when asked again whether he thinks Putin should be considered a friend to the United States.
“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton responded.
Last week, Trump sidestepped questions about his views on a friendship with Putin.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said in a press briefing. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing.”
Trump’s characterization of Putin has sparked backlash from US lawmakers and officials abroad.

“Who is he? He’s the man who has abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine, detained Americans wrongfully, and continues to do so daily,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media.
“Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer added. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.”
“It’s beyond me,” Senator Jeanne Shaheen said in an interview with MS NOW. “I don’t understand the president’s admiration and cozying up to Vladimir Putin, who is a war criminal.”
Trump’s comments also drew rebukes abroad, including from the deputy leader of the rightwing party Reform UK.

“It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake,” Richard Tice told Sky News. “He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”
Trump’s description of ​Putin as a friend also drew criticism from European ​allies of Ukraine. “Mr ‌Putin is ​not our ​friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said.

Separately, Clayton also faced questions about the recent spate of technology outages across the US and said Americans should expect more disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems.
“And ​as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, ⁠interruptions in service,” Clayton said on CNN’s State of the Union program. “That is ⁠going to happen.”

articles.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
articles.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.

blocks.text: The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

items: View the 2026 midterm election results

blocks.text: Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

Wong warns about AI in major foreign policy speech

AI is a foreign policy and national security challenge, Penny Wong will tell parliament this week, raising concerns in a major speech about how the growing technology is being used in war and foreign interference.

Wong will give a substantial foreign policy address to parliament on Tuesday, with advance speech notesy - detailing a focus on artificial intelligence. The foreign minister will warn that AI tools “make that [foreign] interference faster, cheaper and harder to recognise”.
Wong says Australia welcomes investment in AI, but urged a focus on safety - particularly on the international stage.

double quotation markWe must do what we can to ensure that the race to develop frontier AI, concentrated in a handful of companies and countries, does not reward speed over prudence. Australia has helped shape the international order before, in non-proliferation and in online safety. With artificial intelligence, we intend to do it again.

Anika Wells said the government would consult on how to exempt low-risk small businesses – and potentially other services – from the digital duty of care legislation, before it comes into effect 12 months later.

Business groups had called for such a change, but the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry had urged that it be specifically included in the legislation, not worked out later via regulation. ACCI CEO, Andrew McKellar said:

double quotation markA small business should not have to engage lawyers simply to work out whether its website is caught by a regime carrying penalties of more than $100 million. The answer should be in black and white in the legislation.
The Greens are expected to eventually back the bill, but more negotiations will continue this week.
Labor makes new change to digital duty of care
Labor will exempt small businesses from its digital duty of care legislation - a key request from business groups, and potentially another step toward getting the bill passed.
The government is still seeking the support of the Greens on the bill, who want tougher penalties.

The carveout for small businesses from new regulations was not at the top of the Greens’ agenda – they also want a new ombudsman for big tech – but the new update from communications minister Anika Wells shows Labor is in the mood to make deals.
She said:

double quotation markThe intention of the Digital Duty of Care is to put the onus on tech companies to protect Australians from online harms before they occur - not to create additional burden for low-risk small businesses. A low-risk website for a café or bookkeeper is unlikely to cause harm to its users so, once the Digital Duty of Care starts, they will be exempt from the law. We will work closely with small business to get the setting right.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to Guardian Australia’s coverage of Australian politics. Krishani Dhanji will be with us shortly.
Let’s begin.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says
articles.summary:
John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips

Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized…

blocks.text: Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.
On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union, the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.
“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.
Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.
He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

blocks.caption: John Kennedy speaks to the media on 10 November, the day of the Senate Republican caucus leadership elections at the US Capitol in Washington DC. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

blocks.text: “And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.
“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

A former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, Kennedy delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

articles.title: Reporting kutob can save children from online sexual abuse, exploitation, says NGO
articles.summary: Authorities are encouraging people to report even a suspicion that something is wrong or kutob in cases related to online sexual abuse or exploitation of children (OSAEC).

blocks.text: Published November 23, 2026 2:59am
Authorities are encouraging people to report even a suspicion that something is wrong or kutob in cases related to online sexual abuse or exploitation of children (OSAEC).

“Protecting a child begins with something as simple as a kutob, a feeling that something is not right,” said International Justice Mission (IJM) Philippines Community Engagement Director Evelyn Pingul in a statement.

“We don’t need to have proof of abuse before reporting our concerns. Through this campaign, we want to encourage every Filipino to recognize the warning signs, speak up, and take action. One report could make all the difference in a child’s life,” she added.
The IJM said that OSAEC often takes place within the home and is a "pervasive yet underreported crime that is too often dismissed as a private family matter."
A study conducted by IJM Philippines and the University of Nottingham’s Rights Lab showed that one in every 100 Filipino children experienced OSAEC in 2022 alone.
"Children affected by OSAEC may exhibit warning signs such as chronic fatigue from possible late-night livestreaming sessions, social withdrawal due to trauma, or visible distress," the group said.

"Household indicators may also suggest exploitation, including frequent visits to money remittance centers despite having no known family ties abroad, unexplained improvements in lifestyle, or the presence of multiple gadgets and internet-enabled devices without a clear purpose."

Department of Justice Assistant Secretary Michelle Anne Lapuz, in the same statement, encouraged Filipinos to call the DOJ-Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking 1343 Actionline if they notice OSAEC red flags or have information that could help law enforcement initiate an investigation.
“The Philippine government has functional helplines staffed by operators equipped to handle reports of possible OSAEC incidents,” said Lapuz, who leads IACAT.

“Remaining silent despite having kutob or suspicion that a child is being sexually abused and exploited online only enables traffickers to continue their crimes and inflict further trauma on their victims,” she added.

As part of “May Kutob? Mag-Report” campaign, which aims to encourage Filipinos to report suspected OSAEC cases, the IJM and the DOJ-IACAT organized the five-kilometer community run held on Sunday in Ortigas East, Pasig City.
The activity was also supported by Women’s Run PH, the Pasig City Government, the Pasig City Police Office, and the Philippine National Police – Women and Children Protection Center.

Meanwhile, Ambassador Roderick Wols of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Philippines led the ceremonial send-off of the runners. There were also Dutch participants, who are in the country for Muskathlon, a separate endurance event that also supports efforts to combat OSAEC. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
articles.summary: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.

blocks.text: The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.

"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.

In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.

"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.

Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.

Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.

The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".

One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.
The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.

The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

articles.title: COP31 fails to reach major climate deal as talks expose deep divisions
articles.summary: COP31 climate talks fail to make breakthrough on tackling climate change after a row about mentioning fossil fuels.
articles.byline: Mark Poynting, Esme Stallard and Justin Rowlatt

blocks.text: Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".

He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.

But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.

The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.
The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".

"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".
While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.
Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.
He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.
The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.
And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.

In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.
The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.
Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.
But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.

Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.
The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035
But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.
"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work," but acknowledged it "fell short" today.
The UN climate process has "suffered setback before and come back stronger," Stiell told delegates. "It must do so again."

articles.title: COP31 climate talks collapse after member states reject deal for not mentioning fossil fuels
articles.summary: Climate talks collapsed on Sunday at COP31 in Turkey, ending the longest ever UN climate summit with no deal to show for it.

image.caption: This year's UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday with no agreement for the first time since 2009. (Murad Sezer/Reuters)

blocks.text: Climate talks collapsed on Sunday at COP31 in Turkey, ending the longest ever UN climate summit with no deal to show for it.

For more than two weeks, representatives from nearly 200 countries, scientists, businesses and more gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for this year's COP31 conference. The annual UN climate change conference brings together member states to negotiate — and ideally commit to — climate policies that aim to curb global warming. It's the main vehicle through which countries co-ordinate climate action.

But this year, no agreement was met — despite extending heavily into overtime this weekend following Friday's deadline — after the European Union and others rejected the draft put forward by Turkey and Australia.

"There is nothing to do, we did all that we could. Since there are 196 countries, they will make the decision and we will respect their decision," said Turkey's COP31 president Murat Kurum. "There will be no new text from now on."

The lack of a deal means there will be no new action on climate disaster and adaptation financing for developing countries hardest hit by the impacts of climate change as the world is expected to overshoot the 1.5 C target set by the 2015 Paris Agreement, nor any further attempts to rein in the main human drivers of the climate crisis.
It's the first time UN climate talks have failed since 2009, when the conference was held in Copenhagen for COP15.
COP31 fails to reach agreement on deal over omission of fossil fuels from text | Chapman-0900
Fossil fuels weren't mentioned in final draft

Multiple members said the proposed agreement didn't go far enough to match the gravity of the climate crisis — in part because there was no mention of fossil fuels anywhere in the text, despite scientific consensus that they drive global warming.

"At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls short," said a joint European Union statement, delivered by Ireland's Environment Minister Darragh O'Brien and Wopke Hoekstra, European commissioner for climate, net zero and clean growth.
"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change.... And we will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels."

items: Fossil fuel limits cut from latest draft of UN climate deal

blocks.text: Kurum voiced his disagreement with the decision, saying "you should not hurt people in the world who really expect something out of this by just being hung up on one word or phrase."
Oil-producing nations like Saudi Arabia reportedly lobbied to leave out mentions of fossil fuels and instead pushed for the deal to focus on carbon capture and storage technologies.
Big emitters 'profiting' from the planet's destruction: UN chief
A representative for the Saudi delegation told the summit he was surprised that member states voiced resistance to the technology, which is heavily pushed by industry lobbyists.
"If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important, it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions ... will be taken off the table," he said.

Environmentalists have long voiced concerns about overreliance on the tech, saying it could prolong global reliance on fossil fuels. Experts have also warned that carbon capture, while important, can't roll back global warming on its own.

items: Countries vulnerable to climate disaster push for faster, easier access to finance at COP31

blocks.text: Russia was also against mentioning fossil fuels in the agreement.

Panama said it rejected the deal because it failed to acknowledge the scale and urgency of the climate crisis, while Norway's Climate Minister Sigrun Gjerløw Aasland said the draft "takes us backwards."
Climate finance another sticking point
Developing countries, many of which are already struggling with the worst effects of global warming, said the deal didn't allocate enough money to adequately respond to the climate crisis.

"Climate finance must be fully mobilized to drive needed scale and speed in mitigation, adaptation, technology transfer, capacity building and loss and damage," the Philippines delegation said. "A target without means is a promise without a pathway."
Kenya echoed the concern and said Africa wasn't adequately represented.
Who pays when climate disasters strike?

"Africa is not named. The decision rightly speaks of least developed countries and small island states, but not once of Africa's special needs and circumstances," said Kenya's delegation. "Those who took the lead in emissions must take the lead in support. We ask our partners to bring the finance that makes this ambition possible."
Reactions from others trickling in
Reactions from officials, activists and experts already started flooding the internet early Sunday, with many supporting the EU's decision to reject the deal.

"Countries from across regions were right to reject the colossal betrayal that the COP31 co-presidencies tried to pass off as climate action," wrote Amnesty International climate justice policy adviser Ann Harrison. "They refused to accept a deeply unjust text that failed even to name fossil fuels while opening the door to risky technologies that could prolong their use."

items: Poorer nations need $305B US per year to adapt to climate change. UN says they're $277B short

blocks.text: The UN Secretary General António Guterres wrote on X that he's "deeply disappointed" that COP31 ended without consensus.

"I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands. But the setback does not change the facts," he wrote. "The take-home message from COP31 is clear: The world must do much more to confront the climate crisis."
'The planet is not dying, it is being killed' - Thunberg at COP 31
This year, the stakes were high

Notably, this year's summit was the first to take place after the UN's environmental body in October confirmed the rise in global temperature was set to exceed 1.5 C — a threshold countries agreed at Paris climate talks over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify, including through heat waves, floods and droughts.

But it's also marked by competing priorities that threaten to sideline climate action. The collapse this time is against the backdrop of competing crises, including wars and public outcry over the cost of living, that have distracted political attention from the problems of a warming climate largely caused by human activity.
What's next for COP31?

That's it for COP31. The annual summit requires consensus when finalizing agreements. That means: no consensus, no deal. Existing frameworks and agreements established in previous years are still in effect.
The next UN climate summit will take place next year in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

articles.title: Blast on Russian ship in Benghazi a suspected drone attack, say Libyan authorities
articles.summary:
No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia

An explosion on a Russian ship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv, Angelique Chrisafis and agencies

blocks.text: An explosion on a Russian ship docked at the naval base in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya’s eastern-based government has said.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the suspected strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range barrages against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

“Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred onboard a Russian ship docked in the port,” said the administration backed by the military commander Khalifa Haftar. “It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones.”
Authorities in divided Libya’s east said the vessel had stopped at Benghazi port to refuel and ⁠resupply on its way back to Russia, ​under maritime cooperation agreements between ‌the two ‌countries.
Two medical sources said no deaths had been ‌reported from the blast, but there were injuries. The number and nationalities of those injured are not yet known.
There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.

blocks.caption: An explosion on the ship in Benghazi, where it had been refuelling on its way back to Russia. Photograph: X.com

blocks.text: The ‌eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that ​normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.
It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and ⁠a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take ​legal and ​diplomatic measures against ​anyone found responsible.
“The Libyan government will not ​allow Libyan ‌ports, territory or territorial ​waters ​to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the five-year war.
But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians in another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.
Initial reports and footage suggest the ship was struck from above, potentially by a drone, launched no more than a few kilometres away from the target in port.

Russia is close to the Benghazi authorities that control eastern Libya. It uses the port to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean, which has a growing importance after it lost bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was ⁠struck by drones in the ⁠Baltic Sea continued to smoulder ​on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

blocks.caption: Emergency services are working to extinguish a fire onboard the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which was struck in the Baltic Sea. Photograph: Finnish Border Guard/Reuters

blocks.text: The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II ⁠on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly ⁠injured.
On Sunday visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

Pictures ​and video released earlier by the Finnish coastguard showed several ‌vessels spraying the Sparta II with ‌water cannons during the night in an attempt to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.

“Smoke is still coming from the vessel, and ​there is clearly still heat onboard,” said Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, a sea safety officer and commander of the maritime sub-centre Helsinki for the Finnish border guard, at a press conference on Sunday.

Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.
The risk of ⁠further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled ​out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public ​broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last ​week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

articles.title: Libya: Suspected drone attack hits Russian ship in Benghazi

image.caption: The Libyan eastern-based administration said the ship was on its way back to Russia and had stopped in Benghazi to take on fuel and supplies [FILE: November 2020]Image: Abdullah Doma/AFP

blocks.text: An explosion occurred early Sunday on a Russian ship at a naval base in Benghazi in eastern Libya due to a suspected drone attack.
"Initial investigations indicate that the explosion occurred on board a Russian ship docked in the port," the eastern-based Libyan administration said in a statement.
"It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones."
According to medical sources, injuries were reported, but no deaths.

The statement added that, as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based Libyan government, the vessel had stopped at the Benghazi port to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia.

Since the 2011 uprising that overthrew longtime dictator Muammar Gaddafi, Libya has been divided between the UN-supported government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Local authorities condemn attack

The eastern-based administration said the port and naval base facilities in Benghazi, including the warehouses, were safe. They added that normal operations would resume once the fire was under control and the site was secured.

The authorities condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya's sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety. They said they would take legal and diplomatic measures against those responsible and would launch a joint investigation with Russia.
As of Sunday afternoon, no one has claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.

The administration also stressed that Libya was not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine or to any armed conflict beyond its borders. It said that its relations with friendly countries were a sovereign matter.
It said it would not allow "Libyan ​ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international ​conflicts."
Echoes of Russia's war in Ukraine
The incident in Benghazi occurred as Ukrainian forces increased their long-range attacks against Russia, extending far beyond the front lines.
On Saturday, a drone hit a Russian cargo ship in the eastern Baltic Sea near Finnish waters. Finland's border guard said Ukraine carried out the attack.
In March, a Russian tanker was attacked in the Mediterranean near Maltese waters. Libyan officials at the time believed this to be a sea drone attack.

articles.title: Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place | Peter Walker
articles.summary:
Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere

Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday…

blocks.text: Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea.

This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place.

For Tory MPs and activists with a full set of Brexit campaign medals this risks being especially triggering. May’s repeated attempts to cobble together a departure deal that united her party involved repeated humiliations, among them the heaviest-ever parliamentary defeat for a British PM, when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by a majority of 230.

With the afterglow of Boris Johnson’s “get Brexit done” 2019 election triumph now seven years and four prime ministers ago, under Kemi Badenoch the party has opted to do less of, in David Cameron’s resonant phrase, “banging on about Europe”, and instead focus on policy areas such as the economy, social security and defence.

The reasons for this caution are obvious. To begin with, even more ardent Tory Brexiters struggle to articulate any tangible benefits to the UK in the decade since the referendum, beyond slightly niche constitutional points about self-determination.

In her BBC interview, May, who comments sparingly on live political subjects despite being an active Tory peer, did not even try to argue that Brexit had been a success, instead saying that it was impossible to know, given events such as Covid and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and then adding: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union.”

Many voters are much clearer about what they think. Polling suggests that a clear majority of Britons view Brexit as both a failure and a mistake in the first place, with similar support for rejoining the EU, although this depends in part on the pre-conditions for doing so.

This is a product of both lived experience and what pollsters delicately call “demographic churn” – that is, the death of many of the disproportionately older Britons who voted leave and their replacement on the electoral rolls by younger people with more positive views about the EU.
after newsletter promotion
A new constituency-level poll on Brexit sentiment found that hundreds of previously leave-backing areas, including Burnham’s Makerfield seat, now support rejoining.

Of the 632 Commons seats in England, Scotland and Wales, it found that voters in 512 would rejoin the EU, with 47 too close to call. Just 73 areas – slightly over 11% of the total – still want to stay out.

For the Conservatives the battle has not ended. Badenoch will lambast the PM when he sets out his new EU deal in parliament on Monday. Her deputy, Alex Burghart, has already promised that a future Tory government would unpick it.

But make no mistake, Europe is no longer the Conservatives’ defining political thread, and division, as it was for several decades. May might, understandably, be unable to move on from the issue that made her PM and then destroyed her career. But her party, like the country, has no choice.

articles.title: Vouchers for public school students cited
articles.summary: Senators welcomed the enactment of Republic Act 12327, or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, which allows students from overcrowded public schools to enroll in private schools using…

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 12:00am
Elementary students in General Trias, Cavite line up during flag ceremony in this file photo from June of this year.
Edd Gumban

MANILA, Philippines — Senators welcomed the enactment of Republic Act 12327, or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act, which allows students from overcrowded public schools to enroll in private schools using government-funded vouchers.

Signed by President Marcos on Nov. 12 and released on Friday, the law institutionalizes a portable, learner-held voucher system – allowing families to choose government-recognized private schools rather than tying subsidies to school-allocated slots under existing programs.

Priority is given to low-income households, including 4Ps beneficiaries, while persons with disabilities, orphans, indigenous peoples and learners in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas automatically qualify.
Sen. Francis Pangilinan, a co-author of the consolidated Senate measure, stressed that the voucher program must complement – and not replace – state investments in public school infrastructure.
Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano, whose bill was consolidated into the law, said the measure could help ease congestion and bring out-of-school children back to classrooms amid declining enrollment.

articles.title: Philippines, France conduct bilateral maritime exercise
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) through its Naval Command Western Mindanao (NCWM), Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and the French Armed Forces conducted their 3rd Bilateral Maritime…

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 12:00am
The BMCA was conducted under the area of responsibility of the Western Mindanao Command, said NCWM commander Rear Adm. Constancio Arturo Reyes Jr.
Armed Forces of the Philippines / Facebook page

MANILA, Philippines — The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) through its Naval Command Western Mindanao (NCWM), Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and the French Armed Forces conducted their 3rd Bilateral Maritime Cooperative Activity (BMCA) in the Sulu Sea, reinforcing maritime interoperability and defense cooperation between the two forces.

The Philippines deployed the Philippine Navy’s BRP Diego Silang, supported by its AW109 helicopter and other air assets from the Philippine Air Force, such as the C-208B and S-70i Blackhawk helicopters, along with the PCG’s BRP Sarangani during the MCA from Nov. 20 to 22.

France participated with the Floréal-class frigate, the FS Vendémiaire, and a French Navy AS365 Dauphin helicopter, demonstrating the two countries’ shared commitment to strengthening maritime security and cooperation.

“The successful conduct of the 3rd Philippines-France BMCA demonstrated the growing operational cooperation between the two countries and their ability to work together in addressing shared maritime security challenges,” Reyes said.

The AFP said the three-day activity featured communications exercises, personnel exchanges, cross-deck vertical replenishment, division tactics and officer-of-the-watch maneuvers, photo exercise and the cross Visit, Board, Search, and Seizure exercise.

According to the AFP, the activity underscores the “growing defense partnership between the Philippines and France and their shared commitment to a secure, stable, and rules-based maritime environment.”
Air missile defense
Meanwhile, the AFP tested its air and missile defense capabilities during a joint military exercise in Northern Luzon as part of the 10-day AFP Joint Exercise DAGIT-PA.

The AFP conducted an integrated air and missile defense exercise on Nov. 19 at Camp Cape Bojeador in Burgos, Ilocos Norte, testing its ability to detect, track and intercept simulated airborne threats through coordinated operations involving joint air and surface assets.
The 10-day exercise from Nov. 17 to 27 covers various operational areas in Northern Luzon and Palawan.

The DAGIT-PA – which stands for dagat, langit, lupa (sea, air, land) – brings together the Philippine Army, Philippine Air Force, Philippine Navy and Philippine Marine Corps to enhance interoperability and coordination in joint land, air, and maritime operations.
It also integrates the Reserve Force in joint and combined missions, reinforcing unity of effort and the AFP’s ability to respond to evolving security challenges. — Roel Pareño

articles.title: Air traffic disruption readiness eyed
articles.summary: Sen. Raffy Tulfo has filed Senate Resolution 784 to probe the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP)’s readiness to ensure the security, reliability and continuity of air traffic…
