MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Raffy Tulfo has filed Senate Resolution 784 to probe the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP)’s readiness to ensure the security, reliability and continuity of air traffic services in the event of a major communications outage.

The move follows a Nov. 13 incident in the United States that forced the Federal Aviation Administration to declare a nationwide ground stop, temporarily preventing aircraft from taking off for about four hours.
Tulfo recalled the Philippines had experienced a major technical failure on Jan. 1, 2023, involving the CAAP’s Communications, Navigation, and Surveillance/Air Traffic Management system.
The incident disrupted hundreds of flight operations and affected around 65,000 passengers.

As chairman of the Senate committee on public services, Tulfo coordinated with Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon and CAAP chief of aerodrome and air navigation safety oversight Capt. Bryan Balagtas to discuss the issue.

The incident in the US should serve as a wake-up call for the government to strengthen the CAAP’s aviation infrastructure and ensure the reliability of systems essential to the safe, orderly and efficient movement of aircraft, Tulfo stressed.
Tulfo said that it is imperative for the Department of Information and Communications Technology to present its preparedness plan if such wide-scale digital disruptions occur.

articles.title: BusinessWorld Forecast 2027 to tackle economic resilience
articles.summary: As the Philippines looks toward 2027, the economic prospects remain shaped by a range of global and domestic pressures, from geopolitical tensions and energy price volatility to climate risks and…

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — As the Philippines looks toward 2027, the economic prospects remain shaped by a range of global and domestic pressures, from geopolitical tensions and energy price volatility to climate risks and governance concerns.
While growth is expected to recover, businesses and households remain cautious as inflationary pressures and investment constraints shape the country’s economic outlook.
These challenges and opportunities will take center stage at BusinessWorld Forecast 2027, to be held on Nov. 25 at the Grand Ballroom of the Grand Hyatt Manila in Boni-facio Global City, Taguig.

With the theme “Resilience in Disruption,” the forum will bring together policymakers, economists, business executives and industry leaders to discuss how the Philippines can sustain economic growth, navigate emerging risks, and identify opportunities amid an increasingly uncertain global environment.

Hosted by Philippine Stock Exchange head of market education Jester de los Santos, the whole-day event will serve as a platform for thought leaders to share insights on the country’s economic prospects, investment landscape, and strategies for building long-term resilience.

Three keynote speakers will set the tone for the discussions throughout the day. Department of Economy, Planning, and Development Secretary Arsenio Balisacan will deliver a keynote address “The Philippine Economic Outlook: A Path Through Cautious Recovery,” focusing on the country’s growth prospects and the factors that could influence the country’s recovery in 2027.

SM Investments Corp. president and chief executive officer Frederic DyBuncio will share his insights on the country’s growth opportunities amid current economic challeng-es in “Investing for Resilient Philippine Growth”; while iPeople Inc. president and chief operating officer Alfredo Antonio Ayala will talk about addressing skill gaps and pre-paring Filipino workers for an increasingly digital and artificial intelligence-driven workplace in “Human Capital 2.0: Redefining Education and Talent in the Age of AI.”
Panel discussions will delve deeper into issues in trade and logistics, climate resilience, human capital development, political uncertainty and AI.

The first panel discussion, “The Next Evolution of Trade in the Philippines,” will examine how the country can strengthen its logistics network and supply chain connectivity as retail and e-commerce continue to expand. Panelists will include Department of Finance Assistant Secretary Neil Adrian Cabiles, Philippine Exporters Confederation Inc. president and CEO Dr. Sergio Ortiz-Luis Jr., and Reyes Tacandong & Co. Senior Adviser Jonathan Ravelas, CTA.

“Climate Shock: Can the Philippine Economy Stay Resilient?” will be the focus of the second panel discussion. Experts will examine how climate-related disruptions, including typhoons, flooding, extreme heat, and drought, affect business operations, agricultural production, supply chains, and investment decisions.

Among the confirmed panelists are Department of Agriculture Assistant Secretary for operations and adapting Philippine agriculture to climate change National Project Di-rector U-Nichols Manalo, World Bank Senior Country Economist Jaffar Al-Rikabi, ARISE Philippines chairperson and ARISE Global board member Vice-Admiral Alexander Patino Pama AFP (Ret.), and United Nations Laureate and Asian Science Diplomats chairman and president Sci. Dpl. Glenn Banaguas.

The third panel discussion, titled “Between Politics and Prosperity: Navigating an Uncertain Economy,” will examine how political developments and governance concerns could influence investor confidence, economic policies, and business decisions in the year ahead.
Panelists include Stratbase Group founder and chief executive officer Victor Andres Manhit, and political analysts and columnists Rolando Llamas and Andrew James Masigan.

For the final panel, thought leaders will examine how companies can move beyond AI experimentation and translate technological investments into measurable business value, while addressing concerns involving data quality, cybersecurity, implementation costs, and governance, in a discussion titled “AI in Business: Risks versus Rewards.”

Joining the panel are Globe Telecom president and CEO Carl Raymond Cruz; United Nations Development Programme in the Philippines Country Economist Mohamed Sha-hudh; PLDT senior vice president, head of Enterprise Business Group, and Group AI Business lead Patricio Pineda III; and Boston Consulting Group partner Lance Katigbak.

Through these discussions, BusinessWorld Forecast 2027 aims to gather a wide range of perspectives on how the Philippines can move forward through global uncertainty, economic pressures, and structural disruption.
To register for BusinessWorld Forecast 2027, visit https://businessworldforecast.helixpay.ph/.

articles.title: Netanyahu rival condemns settler arson attacks on Palestinian villages in West Bank
articles.summary:
Dozens of militant Israeli settlers raided communities on Saturday night, setting fire to vehicles and several homes

Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem and agencies

blocks.text: Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes were set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars were torched in Deir Abu Mashal.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian man inspects the damage after the attack.  Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA

blocks.text: An ⁠inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.

“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”

Referring to Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”

Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by President Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the Israeli government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.

blocks.caption: The village of Deir Abu Mashal, near Ramallah, was also targeted.  Photograph: Issam Rimawi/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada, and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.

“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.

blocks.caption: A burnt-out car in Kafr Malik. The Israeli politician Yair Lapid said Benjamin Netanyahu’s government had encouraged the attacks.  Photograph: Issam Rimawi/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Israel's Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' in West Bank
articles.summary: Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a recent series of arson attacks in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism." Israeli authorities have opened an investigation into the…

image.caption: Gadi Eisenkot has condemned "Jewish terrorism" in the occupied West BankImage: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP

blocks.text: Israeli authorities were on Sunday investigating arson attacks and vandalism against Palestinian properties and vehicles in the occupied West Bank which Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot condemned as "Jewish terrorism."

Images posted on social media showed vehicles in flames and slogans written on walls reading: "In blood and fire Judea has fallen, in blood and fire Judea will rise again," using a biblical name for the West Bank.
"Settlers attacked the northern area on the outskirts of the village at around two in the morning," Jihad al-Qaq, a local activist, told the AFP news agency.
"They set fire to around eight vehicles and wrote racist slogans on the walls of houses."

Israeli soldiers and police were deployed to the towns of Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashaal, Kafr Malik and Al-Tuwani following the reports, with the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) saying it "strongly condemns" the acts.
Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism'

The suspected arson attacks were condemned by Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who is engaged in post-election negotiations to form a government to replace that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"The night of arson … is Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word, and it must be called what it is," he said.

"Sabotage by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermines regional stability, endangers lives, and severely damages the national security and foreign relations of the State of Israel," he said. Eisenkot used the biblical terms, Judea and Samaria, to refer to the West Bank territories in question.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law, alongside around 3 million Palestinians.

The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967 but attacks against Palestinians have surged in the wake of Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack on Israel. Since then, more than 1,100 Palestinians in the West Bank have been killed by Israeli soldiers or settlers, according to data from the Palestinian Health Ministry.

Local resident Ahmad Ghneimat told the Associated Press that violence had increased after several Israeli settler outposts sprang up in the area. He said settlers have stolen sheep and violently harassed olive harvesters.
"We woke up at 2:30 at night to the sound of explosions [and] seven cars on fire," said Muntasir al-Malik, another resident. "We came out of the houses and panicked."
Eisenkot called for "severe sanctions" to be imposed on the individuals responsible.

Eisenkot's labeling of the violent settlers as "terrorists" follows the use of the same term by the United States' ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, in September. US officials usually reserve the term for Palestinian militants.

articles.title: A small latte and a chat, please: Why this B.C. café owner put conversation on the menu
articles.summary: Registered clinical counsellor Shane Trudell estimates one-third of the population suffers from loneliness — but many people aren't aware of it. A New Westminster café hopes to help.

image.caption: Amrin Satani is the owner of You N Me', a coffee shop in New Westminster that looks to reduce loneliness. (Submitted by Amrin Satani)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Registered clinical counsellor Shane Trudell estimates one-third of the population suffers from loneliness — but many people aren't aware of it. A New Westminster café hopes to help.
Counsellor estimates ⅓ of the population suffers from loneliness
Amrin Satani knows what it’s like to feel alone.
When she came to Canada from India in 2011, she didn’t know anyone. It was a quiet time in her life, she said.
"I know how it feels to have so much in your heart and not have anybody to share that with," she said.
That experience is why she started a business dedicated solely to making sure others have someone to talk to.

According to the Canadian Mental Health Association (CMHA), 13 per cent of Canadians aged 15 and up say they are often lonely. While it affects all demographics, the association says loneliness can affect youth, seniors, people with disabilities and those suffering from addiction in particular.

items: As an immigrant, I know how it feels to be 'lonely and isolated' in my new country

blocks.text: Shane Trudell, a registered clinical counsellor and the clinical director of Nightingale Counselling in Vancouver, said few people seek mental health support specifically for loneliness, but it does often come up during appointments.
He estimates about one-third of the population suffers from loneliness — but it can be tough for people to realize.

"When you’re hungry for food, you learned a long time ago how to be aware of that and to go get a meal," he said. "With loneliness, most people are not aware of it. They feel this social hunger and they don’t know it’s something they should go and fix."
And, he said, the cure for loneliness isn’t one-size-fits-all.

For example, you may be busy at home but in need of connection with people outside the house, he said. Or, you may be dating and meeting new people all the time, but really seeking someone to know you more deeply.
Humanity Café
Satani had always wanted to help others; she planned to study medicine when she first touched down in Canada.
It turned out health care wasn’t for her. But that itch to help people remained.
In 2025, she opened You N Me' (Humanity Café) in New Westminster, B.C.
There, customers have the option to order a drink, something to eat and a conversation.
Amrin Satani chats with a customer at her café in New Westminster. (Submitted by Amrin Satani)

"It's for the days when you feel very happy, or you're feeling lonely, or you want to vent out, you want to celebrate a win, or simply you're just not feeling yourself," she said. "You want just another company and you feel that at least I had somebody whom I can just sit with or have coffee with."
Satani sits with customers who ask for a conversation whenever she can.
"I love it. It has no money attached to it. It has no finance attached to it. It has no tip attached to it, but I think it's the best thing people can buy here at the café."

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: While everything, including connecting with others, often happens online nowadays, Trudell said he’s encouraged by the concept of Satani’s café.

"I love that it’s something that’s in person," he said. "There’s kind of a high bar for entry. A person has to be willing to say, 'Hey I’d like to order a conversation.' You’re more likely to get people who are going to benefit from the experience."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Courtney Dickson is a journalist with CBC News based in Vancouver, covering stories throughout B.C. She has previously worked for CBC in Kamloops and Toronto. She has won Radio Television Digital News Association awards locally and nationally, and in 2022, won a Webster Award.
With files from Izzy Morgan

articles.title: Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war
articles.summary:
UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues

A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait…

blocks.text: A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.
Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.
According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.

An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”
The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.

He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”
The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.

Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.
The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.
Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use
articles.summary: After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

image.caption: Delegates gather around the COP31 president Turkey Murat Kurum. Turkey and Australia hosted what some say was the worst UN climate summit everImage: Khalil Hamra/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," said Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.
He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required."

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.
"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation said.
The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."

Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.
Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.
Deep divisions over climate finance

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing.

Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.
COP31 talks run overtime as fossil fuel divisions deepen
Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.
"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs."
Fossil fuel exit on the sidelines
Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation."

At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels.

But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance.

"COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'"
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?
The push for global electrification
The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.
It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey.

Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.
Hottest ever climate conference

The talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot."

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”
It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.
Maldives environment minister: 'We are not going to live in the dark'

Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text said the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.
Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu said carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve."
A year of extremes
The stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.
At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, said his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

"We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation."
With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.
Australia's climate dilemma: selling nature while exporting coal

articles.title: Elite B.C. snowboarder's injury highlights financial strain of Olympic dreams
articles.summary: Prince George's Meryeta O'Dine suffered fractured ankle in a devastating crash during a snowboard cross training run in February and was unable to compete at the 2026 Olympics.

image.caption: Snowboarder Meryeta O'Dine fractured her ankle during a training run at the 2026 Winter Olympics. She says the cost of recovery, being unable to work, and the ongoing expenses of training have left her in debt. (Meryeta O'Dine/GoFundMe)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Prince George's Meryeta O'Dine suffered fractured ankle in a devastating crash during a snowboard cross training run in February and was unable to compete at the 2026 Olympics.
Meryeta O'Dine competed in the 2018 and 2022 Winter Olympics before fracturing her ankle at the 2026 games
A debilitating injury that an elite B.C. snowboarder sustained while representing her country has highlighted the financial challenges of pursuing an Olympic dream.
Prince George's Meryeta O'Dine took home a pair of bronze medals in snowboard cross at the 2022 games in Beijing, and travelled to Italy to compete in the 2026 Milano-Cortina Olympics.
But she suffered a fractured ankle in a devastating crash during a snowboard cross training run in February and was unable to compete.
First aid workers treat Meryeta O'Dine after a fall during training at the 2026 Winter Olympics. (Submitted by Meryeta O'Dine)
"I was home by the time my event was happening," O'Dine said. "It was horribly upsetting."
Adding to the heartbreak of missing the competition was financial strain.
O'Dine said she was unable to fulfil contracts and attract future sponsors, and was injured badly enough she couldn't work for five months.
Meanwhile, travel, training and rehab bills have piled up.
"I'm essentially kind of in crisis mode right now," she said. "It's more than what I currently have in my bank account, and the bills I have coming up."
O'Dine said people often don't realize that most competitive athletes, outside of the high-paying professional leagues, are already scrambling to make ends meet.
Canadian Olympic snowboarder Meryeta O'Dine is seen dressed for competition. (Submitted by Meryeta O'Dine)
Big money sponsorships are hard to come by unless you top the podium, while international travel and a weak Canadian dollar make training and competition expensive, she said.
"Genuinely, I've never had a year where I haven't ended my season in debt, because things always cost a little bit more than we are expecting them to," O'Dine said.
Nationwide issue
Advocates have long raised concerns about funding for Canadian athletics.
Can Fund, a charity that helps financially support Canadian athletes, says almost two-thirds of applicants to its program work part-time jobs, on top of their training, just to get by.
It says three in five of those athletes are in debt and live with a negative net income.
"The average athlete goes $30,000 to $80,000 in debt," said Can Fund founder Jane Roos.
A former athlete herself, Roos said she started the program after suffering an injury as a way to help other competitors.

items: Federal government announces $60M in additional funding to national sports organizations
Why the Canadian sport system is in financial disarray

blocks.text: "I've never met an athlete who wants a handout," she said. "But let me tell you, when they win the medals, we sure claim them as our own and we tell the world how happy we are, and proud of them we are.
"And you know what? You can't be the best in the world at anything without support, right?"
In July, the federal government announced it was adding $3 million to the Athlete Assistance Program (AAP), which provides a monthly living and training allowance to about 1,900 qualified athletes.
The funding will see monthly support for senior athletes increase by 5.5 per cent to $2,300 per month.
Feds announce additional $60M in sports funding
New funding from Ottawa

Last month, Ottawa unveiled about $60 million in supplemental funding for 62 governing sports bodies, part of a new five-year $660-million sport funding package, including a $2.86-million boost to the Canadian Snowboard Federation.
At the time, Snowboard Canada CEO Dustin Heise described the new funding as "transformational."

items: Meryeta O'Dine had to work through her grief before she could win Olympic bronze
Canadian snowboarder Meryeta O’Dine to miss Olympics with fractured ankle

blocks.text: O'Dine said she wouldn't be able to compete without the funding she receives from the AAP, and is grateful for the increase.
But she said it's still not enough to cover her travel and out-of-country training expenses, and is currently fundraising to keep her dream alive.
Meanwhile, she isn't letting funding challenges get in the way of her passion for snowboarding.
She's currently in Austria training.
"I don't think I've ever been so excited for a season," she said. "The training just this past week on snow has been absolutely incredible."
With files from Catherine Hansen, Andrew Kurjata and Daybreak Kamloops

articles.title: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected
articles.summary:
EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ after two weeks of fierce negotiations

•
articles.byline: Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn in Antalya

blocks.text: The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that campaigners have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and many developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be the “cover decision”, or main outcome, of the Cop.

In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

blocks.caption: Darragh O’Brien (centre) and Wopke Hoekstra, the EU climate commissioner, speak outside a plenary session at Cop31 on Sunday. Photograph: Khalil Hamra/AP

blocks.text: His intervention was met by applause from the hall, and was later followed by similar objections from Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway.
“This feels like a real line in the sand moment. Countries are standing up to fossil fuel interests and saying no,” said Bill Hare, the chief executive of the advisory group Climate Analytics.
Saudi Arabia defended the decision to include CCS in the text. Other countries, including the Africa group, China and Pakistan, also did not object to the deal, despite some having reservations.
after newsletter promotion

Close to 200 countries have been meeting in Antalya for a fortnight under the joint presidencies of Turkey and Australia, with the overrunning talks marked by long periods of deadlock as countries failed to find common ground.

For many participants, these talks exposed a failure of collective will, particularly of the rich world, to confront the urgency of the climate crisis. Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, while African ministers made a dramatic intervention on Friday saying: “We did not come here to beg.”

Mohamed Adow, the director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, summed up the view of many on Friday when he said: “The Cop presidents want to tell us this has been a great Cop. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst Cop ever.”

On Sunday, he added: “The EU has rejected this text, but it cannot wash its hands of the wreckage it helped create.... For countries facing failed harvests, destroyed homes and mounting debt, this amounts to abandonment by the wealthy nations most responsible for the crisis.
“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves.”

While extreme weather around the world has worsened this year, claiming tens of thousands of lives in heatwaves, in disasters such as the glacier collapse in Nepal, and in droughts and floods worsened by the supercharged El Niño, the slow speed of the climate negotiations appalled even veteran participants.

“There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues. That to me is very frustrating,” said Mary Robinson, a former president of Ireland and former UN climate envoy, as the talks neared their scheduled close. “We have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

articles.title: COP31: Climate deal 'not adopted,' summit president says
articles.summary: The summit was extended as nations worked to reach a deal, but they couldn't agree on including fossil fuels. European nations, small island states and activists have criticized oil-producing…
articles.byline: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez, Emmy Sasipornkarn, Nik Martin, Dmytro Hubenko, Patrick Große, Mark Hallam, Karl Sexton

image.caption: Despite weeks of talks and an extension, a deal has remain elusiveImage: Khalil Hamra/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: November 22, 2026
COP31 fails to agree climate deal amid fossil fuel rift

blocks.caption: Weeks of tense negotiations have failed to yield a dealImage: Murad Sezer/REUTERS

blocks.text: The COP31 climate summit has failed to agree on a final joint declaration.
During a plenary session, the summit's Turkish president acknowledged there would be no climate deal.

"I understand that there is no agreement on this text. For that reason, these decisions have not been adopted," Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, told a closing plenary in the Mediterranean city of Antalya.

The rift centered on whether to include the phaseout of fossil fuels in the final declaration. Scientists say the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas is the main cause of global warming.
European nations, smaller island states and climate activists have criticized oil-producing countries for the omission.

articles.title: B.C. couple lose business in devastating fire, credit volunteer firefighters with saving their home
articles.summary: A West Kootenay couple is counting their blessings after a massive fire destroyed their home-based mechanic shop in Burton, B.C. — and came dangerously close to taking their house with it.

image.caption: Becky and Sandy Shilka saw their mechanic shop in the small community of Burton, B.C., go up in flames on Nov. 11. (Submitted by Becky Shilka)

blocks.text: British Columbia
A West Kootenay couple is counting their blessings after a massive fire destroyed their home-based mechanic shop in Burton, B.C. — and came dangerously close to taking their house with it.
Small community of Burton, B.C., rallying around couple after fire destroys mechanic shop
Becky and Sandy Shilka were getting ready for bed shortly after 9 p.m. on Nov. 11, when the lights flickered inside their home.
Sandy went outside to investigate, smelled smoke, and followed it into his adjacent mechanics garage.
"I ran inside and there was no fire inside," Sandy recalled. "And went outside and could see fire in the wall."
Volunteer firefighters had to spring into action in Burton to fight the flames at the mechanic shop. (Submitted by Becky Shilka)
As the shop's sprinklers activated, Sandy rushed back home and pounded on the door to alert Becky, who called the fire department.
"When it's happening to you, you're like, no way," she said. "You don't even know what you need. You don't even, like, you can't even think."
Volunteer fire department scrambled
Burton Deputy Fire Chief Chris Jackins says volunteer crews were rolling in less than seven minutes after receiving the call.
"My poor wife didn't even put socks on for the fire. That's how quickly we tried to get up here," he told CBC's Radio West host Sarah Penton.
LISTEN | Becky and Sandy describe the fire:
Radio West13:55Friends, neighbours come together to save home from massive fire in West Kootenays
But oil and fire accelerants had quickly turned the smoking garage into an inferno.
"We saw the sky red, so we knew what we were coming to was extreme," Jackins said.

"When we pulled in, you could see the flames were probably about 40 feet [12 metres] tall.... It was all metal sheeting, so the fire was actually being held within the building, but it was coming out of the doors and the windows had exploded."
A firefighter says the heat from the blaze on Nov. 11 was so intense it began melting nearby vehicles. (Submitted by Becky Shilka)
The heat was so intense it began igniting nearby outbuildings and melting vehicles.
With the shop fully engulfed and the potential for explosions from materials inside, firefighters knew there was little chance of saving it.
Instead, they concentrated on protecting the couple's adjacent home.
The wreckage of a vehicle is seen next to the Shilkas' burned mechanic shop. (Submitted by Becky Shilka)
Looking at the damage the following morning, Jackins could see the fascia beneath the home's roofline had been badly charred.
"I think we are probably two or three minutes away from losing the house," he said. "You know, they say in the fire department that seconds matter. It really did."
A closer community
For Becky, watching friends and neighbours rush to protect their home was an emotional experience.
"It's just like seeing love in action," she said, fighting back tears.
The support has continued well beyond the night of the fire.
Becky Shilka, left, held back tears as she spoke alongside her husband Sandy, centre, and Burton's Deputy Fire Chief Chris Jackins. (CBC)

Neighbours have brought an excavator to help clear the wreckage, while others delivered food and offered emotional support. One community member showed up with a brand-new freezer after realizing the couple had nowhere to store the food.
The mechanic shop was Sandy's full-time business, equipped with a vehicle hoist and the tools he needed to make a living.
Jackins says it was more than just a community business. Sandy was also the mechanic who donated his time maintaining the department's fire trucks.
"He's one of us," Jackins said.

"[A small] community is something that you build and Sandy and Becky are a huge part of that. And when emergency happens and devastation happens, it's amazing to see it come together and to see the community support."

items: More stories from the B.C. Interior

blocks.text: The Shilka's losses are compounded by the fact they had no insurance on either the business or home. Becky says insuring the shop alone would have cost about $10,000 a year.
Despite losing his livelihood and much of his equipment, Sandy has already received offers of donated lumber for a possible rebuild and tools from a friend.
The community has started a local fundraiser.
For now, Becky says they're focusing on what they still have rather than what they've lost.
"Whenever our minds start going down that dark hole, we just come back to the fact that we still have a home," she said.
"We got to sleep in our own beds the night of, and we got to drink coffee right where we're sat now in the morning. And we're just so grateful for that."
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.
With files from Sarah Penton and Radio West

articles.title: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments
articles.summary: Officials have publicly questioned whether Musiala will ever fully recover from a debilitating neurological condition and queried the validity of his contract, prompting criticism from fans, media…

image.caption: Former Bayern CEO and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge (background) has led public criticism of Jamal Musiala (foreground)Image: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the space of just two days this weekend, Bayern Munich were held to a 1-1 draw by FC Cologne, saw Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane ruled out until the new year with a serious ankle injury and lost first place in the Bundesliga to rivals Borussia Dortmund.

But even those setbacks – as well as the return of head coach Vincent Kompany to the sideline following health issues – have been overshadowed by explosive public comments made by Bayern club bosses regarding young attacker and Germany international Jamal Musiala.
What is wrong with Jamal Musiala?
Back in July 2025, Musiala suffered a fractured fibula and a broken ankle at the Club World Cup.

Since then, the 23-year-old has been battling to recover not only from that injury but also with a debilitating neurological condition diagnosed as "absence seizures" which led him to collapse on the pitch in two consecutive pre-season games in August this year.
Musiala has struggled to replicate the sort of form which led to a well-remunerated contract extension in January 2025, prior to the ankle injury and the seizures.
The situation has now prompted a series of controversial public remarks from the Bayern hierarchy seemingly questioning the validity of that contract.
What have Bayern Munich officials said?

"It is well known that he has a contract which contains some considerable sums," former chief executive and current supervisory board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge told broadcaster Sky on Friday evening following the 1-1 draw with Cologne, in which Musiala had made a 20-minute substitute appearance.

blocks.caption: Bayern head coach Vincent Kompany (who himself has just recovered from a serious infection) brought Musiala on as a substitute against CologneImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "It's in all of our interest that he comes back, ideally in top form, but what happens if that's not the case?" asked Rummenigge, adding that Musiala's condition "leads us to suspect, unfortunately, that it will be difficult [for him] to return to the level that he has often shown in this stadium" and that "then we of course have to think about the finances."
Rummenigge suggested a need for Bayern to hold talks with Musiala, his family and his representatives because "such sums are, with respect, no longer justifiable."

Asked whether Bayern would consider selling Musiala, Rummenigge said he considered it unlikely that any club would be prepared to buy the player out of his new contract, which is set to run until 2030 and which reportedly sees Musiala earn up to €30 million per year.
"I cannot imagine that Jamal would leave the club or that any other club would buy him under these conditions," said Rummenigge. "And that is a problem."

Rummenigge was not the first senior Bayern official to express such doubts. Earlier this month, former club president Uli Hoeness had told local broadcaster Bayrischer Rundfunk that Musiala's situation presented the club with a "dilemma."

"He has an illness which cannot be cured but which can be somewhat controlled through medication," said Hoeness, who also sits on Bayern's supervisory board, questioning "whether he will ever regain the ability he once had" and stating that "he continues to receive money."

Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen has also weighed in, telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper last week: "We all have a responsibility towards the club and we all hope that Jamal will come back. Of course this will take time. We will assess the situation and speak to his family and management. Either we'll all be happy that the old Jamal [will return] or, if he becomes a different [player], we'll have to hold talks."
FIFPRO: 'Bayern should know better'
The comments by Hoeness, Dreesen and Rummenigge landed like a bombshell in Germany and beyond.

The global players' union FIFPRO issued a statement on Saturday slamming what they called "a coordinated strategy to put pressure on Musiala and his representatives ahead of any negotiations," highlighting Bayern's "duty of care" towards their player, and stating: "A club of Bayern's standing should know better."

"Across professional football, uncertainty about a player's future can take a toll on their mental health, particularly when they are recovering from injury," the statement continued. "Making Musiala's health and future a matter of public debate adds to that pressure. Contracts are there to be respected. An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise."

Former Bayern Munich and Germany defender Lothar Matthäus also criticized the club, saying in his role as a pundit for Sky: "I've been a bit shocked throughout the entire week. It started with Uli Hoeness, continued with Jan-Christian Dreesen, and yesterday Karl-Heinz Rummenigge chose the strongest words of all. I have enormous respect for Karl-Heinz. I've known him for over 30 years. But he chose those statements very deliberately. The person who suffers most from all this is Jamal Musiala."

The comments by the Bayern bosses also came just hours ahead of the club's annual general meeting on Saturday, where club members – who hold a majority 70% stake in the club in accordance with German football's "50+1" ownership rule – took to the stand to criticize the club's hierarchy.
One member, professional neurologist Jonatan Hoffmann, expressed his "absolute respect" for Musiala and said that patients suffering from such conditions require "support."

He said Musiala had received such support from head coach Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl, but said Hoeness', Dreesen's and Rummenigge's comments were "not helpful" and had "little to do with the much talked about Bayern Munich family" – earning considerable applause from fellow members.

blocks.caption: Bayern Munich member Jonatan Hoffmann, a neurologist by trade, criticized his club's executivesImage: Harry Langer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bayern president: 'Musiala will get time and support'

Bayern president Herbert Hainer, the club's most senior elected official, attempted to deescalate the situation, responding to Hoffmann by saying: "Health and difficult situations are fundamentally always taken into account at FC Bayern."

Indeed, Bayern have recently been praised for their considerate handling of captain Joshua Kimmich following the unexpected death of his father, and of head coach Kompany, who returned to the touchline against Cologne on Friday following a month-long absence after collapsing due to a particularly serious viral infection.
"When it comes to Jamal, we all want the old Jamal back as he was before his injury," said Hainer. "And he will receive all the support and time he needs from the club."

Speaking on the sidelines of the meeting, chief executive Dreesen also attempted to row back on his comments, insisting to reporters that he and his colleagues had not been trying to put Musiala under pressure.

"We all want Jamal to return to the old Jamal. He needs time. We've said that several times. And he must get that. And then we'll see how things look in the new year," he said, adding that there was no need "to talk about the contract."

President Hainer also dismissed questions from journalists as to whether Bayern felt they had been misled by Musiala's agents before offering him a new contract, inferring that the player's representatives may have known about his neurological condition.
"I absolutely do not think that anyone knew beforehand," Hainer insisted.

blocks.caption: Bayern club president Herbert Hainer attempted to diffuse the situation at Saturday's annual general meetingImage: Harry Langer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German media criticize Bayern

But the public criticism has continued. Leading German sports publication Kicker said it was understandable for the Bayern bosses to be frustrated but called their approach "irresponsible" and said their anger "harms the wrong person" in Musiala.

"He can't help his injuries or neurological condition," wrote editor-in-chief Matthias Dersch. "Musiala is only 23 … and is in the most difficult phase of his career. We cannot imagine how he must be feeling, his insecurities and perhaps also fears about his health and his future. And no: the amount of money he earns is no cure."

German football magazine 11Freunde said the Musiala case offered "a glimpse into the abyss of professional football … an unembellished look behind the scenes of a business which is generally portrayed only as glamorous and exciting … into a shadow world where human beings are damned to function … where the value of a person is measured only by their ability to perform over and over again … That's football: capitalism in its purest form."

Meanwhile, the business of football continues. Borussia Dortmund capitalized on Bayern's draw to go top of the Bundesliga with a 1-0 win away at Borussia Mönchengladbach, Harry Kane underwent an operation on a torn ankle ligament but will be out until the new year, meaning he will miss Bayern's trip to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday.
And the young Jamal Musiala will continue to battle the effects of serious physical and neurological conditions.

articles.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
articles.summary:
Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long

British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to…

blocks.text: British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products.

The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks.
The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs.
However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.
“Nobody’s going to believe this until it has actually physically happened,” said Iain Barbour, the operations director of the Scottish seed potato producer Jamieson Brothers.

Seed potatoes were not included in the post-Brexit trade deal after the two sides disagreed over certification, halting exports from the UK to the EU despite Scottish seed potatoes’ high health status classification.

The exclusion particularly hit the Scottish industry, whose farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world, as well as growers in northern England. Scottish seed potato farmers previously accounted for three-quarters of UK production and the sector was worth about £112m a year.

Ireland and the EU represented a fifth of Jamieson Brothers’ trade before Brexit. The company particularly suffered from the loss of the Irish business, given it grew many varieties that were popular on plates in the north and south of Ireland.

blocks.caption: Scottish potato farmers were among the biggest exporters for the production of chips and crisps in the world before Brexit. Photograph: Skully/Alamy

blocks.text: While the company adapted its business to start packing work that would have previously been carried out in the EU, Barbour estimates this change cost about £500,000.
“We evolved, we worked with more partners and that’s what kept the business going,” Barbour said.

Barbour is looking forward to supplying his Irish customers once againHowever, he said it would take at least three years until he could revive varieties that were no longer being grown and were instead stored in a seed bank.

“A lot of Scottish farmers stopped producing varieties that were popular in Ireland as they weren’t desired in England. Varieties that had been going about 100 years were killed off in a couple of years,” he said. “So we’ll have to look at bringing them back.”

The planned implementation of the food deal in March 2028 would also be “a couple of months late for the trade”, given most sales happen at the start of the year and the crops needs to be grown in advance.
Barbour anticipates most growers will be wary and will only fully resume trading in 2029. “People are obviously going to be a little bit hesitant to grow anything until it’s 100% official,” he said.

blocks.caption: Devon’s Offshore Shellfish has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite post-Brexit red tape. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

blocks.text: British exporters of live bivalve molluscs – the collective term for shellfish including mussels, oysters, clams, cockles and scallops – hope the deal will give the sector a shot in the arm.
The industry is small and specialised. It was valued at less than £12m a year before Brexit, but it is crucial for some coastal communities.

Offshore Shellfish, a family-run business produces rope-grown mussels in the waters of Lyme Bay, Devon, has managed to continue exporting to its European customers despite the administrative burden and occasional blocks by French customs.
after newsletter promotion

The company exports the vast majority of the blue mussels it produces. It sends to the Netherlands for processing, before most end up in restaurants or on supermarket shelves in Belgium, where they are prized as a key ingredient in moules-frites, one of the country’s national dishes.

blocks.caption: Offshore Shellfish’s Sarah Holmyard says the deal’s provisions are ‘a huge win for us’. Photograph: Offshore Shellfish

blocks.text: Sarah Holmyard, the commercial director of Offshore Shellfish, said the most important detail was an assurance that the deal would allow live bivalve molluscs to be exported even if they did not come from waters with the highest quality rating.

Offshore Shellfish’s farms are in waters which are considered “class A” for most of the year, but before the new SPS deal, any change in water quality to “class B” could have temporarily halted exports.
“That’s a huge win for us because we’ve been pushing and pushing and pushing for that,” Holmyard said.

However, the deal will come too late for those UK shellfish producers that have closed down since Brexit. Three out of four mussel fishing companies in the Menai strait, the channel that separates the north Wales mainland from the island of Anglesey, stopped trading after exports became too difficult.

The promised end of physical border checks on dairy, fish and meat products was welcomed by Rich Clothier, the managing director of Wyke Farms. The Somerset-based cheese and butter maker exports about a quarter of its cheddar to the EU, particularly France, Germany and Spain.

blocks.caption: Rich Clothier, the managing director of cheesemaker Wyke Farms, says the deal ‘will save a huge amount of cost and product waste’. Photograph: Josh Campbell

blocks.text: Dairy exports to the EU have been less contentious since Brexit than seed potatoes or mussels, but not without challenges. The removal of veterinary checks is viewed as a significant benefit by Clothier.

“It’s a very bureaucratic process to get everything signed off, in what is not a very modern sort of system,” he said. “The agreement will save a huge amount of cost and product waste as well, because these are perishable.

“Any reduction in friction saves cost, it makes business more efficient. But it is really frustrating that it’s going to take so long [to be implemented] because, to be honest, we’re all pretty aligned anyway.”

articles.title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
articles.summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.

blocks.text: "As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

articles.title: Indian opposition party’s youth wing warns of more Meta protests after police clashes
articles.summary:
Members of Congress party clashed with police outside tech company’s offices on Friday

The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal…

blocks.text: The youth wing of India’s main opposition Congress party warned of more protests against Meta’s removal of some of its members’ ⁠accounts, ⁠a day after clashing with ​police outside the tech firm’s locals offices.

In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters ‌carrying placards and chanted slogans as they stormed into ‌the building that houses Meta’s offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress’s X account.
The Indian Youth Congress on Saturday posted warnings on X that it would “storm your offices across the country and stage protests” unless the Instagram accounts of its leaders were restored.

Two such accounts were restored after Friday’s protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for ⁠the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down ​on government orders, he added.
India is Meta’s biggest market by users and the company declined to comment on Friday’s demonstrations.

blocks.caption: Congress members burn signs during a protest in Mumbai. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

blocks.text: Debate is growing in India about potential ⁠risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Narendra Modi’s government to remove social media content it objects to. India’s IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Meta has said it restricts ​content in India to comply with local laws.

Modi’s government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety ⁠or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing accounts.

A video ‌from Friday’s demonstration showed protesters spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office and clashing with security guards who tried to stop them.
In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading “restore youth Congress accounts”, online posts showed.

An opposition politician from Telangana state criticised Congress workers over what he called vandalism at Meta’s Hyderabad office, saying it ​had undermined the city’s reputation as a safe destination for businesses.

blocks.caption: Police clash with Youth Congress members at a protest in Hyderabad. Photograph: Indian Youth Congress/IYC/Reuters

blocks.text: Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi’s ruling party, also criticised Congress’ actions on Saturday, saying they had “not only vandalised and destroyed Meta’s office in Hyderabad” but were also “flaunting it on social media”.
“This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies,” he wrote.

Reporters Without Borders has ​said the removal of journalistic content from social media ​has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media ​companies hardly any time to review ‌and decide on takedown requests.
In ​February, Modi’s government ordered social media companies ​to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline.
Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4m posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the whole of 2025.
“The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content … based on local law requirements,” Meta said.

articles.title: Quebecor CEO defends Telus bid, cites falling wireless prices and Canada's sovereignty

image.caption: Quebecor president and CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau waits to speak at the Freedom Mobile Arch concert venue in Vancouver on June 5. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Quebecor CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau is defending his company's $31-billion bid to buy Telus amid concerns over competition in Canada's telecom sector, arguing the cost of wireless plans is dropping and non-Canadian companies are trying to expand.
Montreal-based telecom has submitted $31-billion proposal for Telus to review
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 22, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 31 minutes ago

Quebecor Inc. CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau is defending his company's $31-billion bid to buy Telus Corp. amid concerns over competition in Canada's telecom sector, arguing the cost of wireless plans is dropping and non-Canadian companies are trying to expand.

"Telecom assets are strategic for our country — we all know this. And then therefore, we need to make sure that we're going to be on the same footing," Péladeau said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live airing Sunday morning.

The Montreal-based telecom, media and entertainment company said on Monday that it submitted a non-binding proposal to Telus in June to serve as a basis for negotiations and that the Vancouver-based corporation is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month.

Quebecor's move comes three years after the federal government approved Rogers Communications' acquisition of Shaw Communications on the condition that Freedom Mobile be sold to Quebecor to preserve a four-player market.

Péladeau told CBC chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that his company has been servicing Freedom Mobile and the Canadian market "pretty efficiently, and our results talk by themselves. We look forward to being able to continue to do the same with the Telus assets."
Quebecor's $31B bid to buy Telus: What it means for your phone bill
Asked how a merger of this size would help with Canadians' wireless costs, Péladeau said prices continue to fall after his company acquired Freedom Mobile.
"Our earnings are growing, our free cash flow is growing," he said. "Why would you change a successful strategy?"

According to Canada's annual telecom report, consumer prices for cellular services declined in recent years but ticked back up in 2025. Canada still had some of the highest wireless prices compared with other developed countries.

items: If Quebecor buys Telus, less competition could mean higher cellphone bills, experts say

blocks.text: Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company. With its $14.77-billion market capitalization and Telus's $21.72-billion market cap, the potential deal would make Quebecor larger than Rogers or Bell by that metric.

Péladeau also framed the proposed bid as a way of protecting Canada's sovereignty, noting Elon Musk's satellite internet provider Starlink services parts of the Canadian market and is likely hungry to expand its operations.

"[Starlink's] business model is the world, like Netflix's business model was the world," Péladeau said, adding that Netflix "destroyed a Canadian industry" despite not having a licence with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).
Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company, with a $14.77-billion market capitalization. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Telus says it has formed a special committee to review the offer and determine the value of the potential deal. So far, the committee has discovered a number of "significant risks," John Manley, the chair of Telus's board of directors, said in a statement on Monday issued by the company.
Telus also takes issue with how the Quebecor proposal values the company.
Manley said Telus would continue to engage with Quebecor, the government and regulatory authorities about those concerns while exploring alternatives.
The federal perspective so far

In its news release on Monday, Quebecor acknowledged that Canada's Competition Bureau — along with other authorities, such as the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada — will need to approve the deal.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said more competition, lower prices and better service would be key to any decision regarding the telecom sector.
'This is the last thing we need': NDP asks feds to block Quebecor's Telus bid

Carney declined to comment directly on Quebecor's proposal but said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition with fewer players. He didn't elaborate further.
Péladeau said he doesn't think anyone would disagree with Carney's comments, noting that even if there are three Canadian companies, there will still be other competition, like Starlink.
On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party has not yet seen the proposal but would study it and base its judgment on the principle of lowering prices for consumers.

items: Why Quebecor wants to buy Telus and what it could mean for British Columbians

blocks.text: Poilievre also criticized Carney's comments, saying he has never seen "any economist anywhere in the world say that oligarchies ultimately bring prices down.... Once again, Mr. Carney favours the corporate power brokers over the consumers."
NDP Leader Avi Lewis has called on the Competition Bureau to cancel the sale, saying it will increase costs for consumers and trigger layoffs.

"We already pay some of the highest cellphone prices in the world," he said. "I just think it's so obvious to the vast majority of people who are suffering under this cost-of-living crisis that this is just yet another thing where the big boys just ... swallow up another company."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Lopez Steven is an associate producer for CBC's The House and a digital writer with CBC Politics. He was also a 2024 Joan Donaldson Scholar and a graduate of Carleton University. You can reach him at benjamin.steven@cbc.ca or find him on X at @bensteven_s.
